BOMBAY

Pages 9-14

This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, which is the seat of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> for the western <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, is situated in Lat. 18° 57', <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 72° 53'. Its length from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south is eight miles, and its breadth about three. It is separated from the mainland by an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and forms, in conjunction with the adjacent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Salsette on the north, and Colaba with Old Woman's Island on the south, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, commodious, and well-sheltered harbour. The two islands on the south, separated from Bombay and from each other by narrow channels, have been united by causeways, which are now entirely raised above the sea at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. To the north Bombay is connected with Salsette also, by a causeway with an arched <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>; and, more recently, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> causeway has been thrown over the strait for the purposes of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> India <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">Peninsula</a> railway. The islands thus linked together form a continuous <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-BREAKWATER">breakwater</a>, stretching for several miles from north to south. Near the southern extremity of Colaba Island stands the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of circular form, rising from the sea to the height of 150 feet, and showing its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> at the distance of twenty-one miles. Within the harbour, and about a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Bombay, is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a> Island, N.E. of which, and at the distance of three miles, is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-BUTCHER">Butcher</a> Island. Abreast of the latter, but more to the eastward, lies the celebrated Island of Elephanta. Caranja Island, to the southward of Elephanta, on the east side of the harbour, and opposite its entrance, is of considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, being four miles long and nearly two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; it is covered with woods, and has little elevation with the exception of two remarkable hills called Great and Little Caranja Hills. Besides the above there are two small islands, Oondaree and Kundaree, lying at the entrance of the harbour. The town of Bombay within the fort is nearly a mile in length, from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> Gate to that of the Bazaar, and about a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a mile broad in the widest part, from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> across the Green to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> Gate, which is nearly in the centre between the Apollo and the Bazaar Gates. There are likewise two gates towards the sea, having commodious wharfs and cranes built out from each, with a landing-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for passengers. Between these gates is Bombay Castle, a regular quadrangle, built of hard and durable stone, and having the advantage, in one of the bastions, of a large reservoir of water. The fortifications are extensive, and they have been improved in proportion as the place has risen into greater importance from its increasing trade. They have received a considerable accession of strength from Dungansoe Hill, which commanded the town, having been included within the fort; and towards the sea they are extremely strong, the harbour being completely commanded by ranges of batteries placed one above another. In the centre of the town is a large open space called the Green, around which are many large, well-built, and handsome houses. Here is also the church, which has an extremely neat and light appearance; and on the left of the Church Gate is the government-house, which is a showy edifice, but liable to the inconvenience of having the largest apartment in each <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> a passage-room to the others. On the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the Church Gate is the bazaar, which is crowded and populous. Here the native <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> reside; and at the entrance to the street stands the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, which is a handsome building. In the year 1803 this part of the town was greatly injured by a destructive fire, which destroyed nearly three-fourths of the bazaar, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, custom-house, and many other public buildings, besides <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of immense value belonging to native merchants. Another extensive conflagration occurred in 1845, when nearly 200 houses were destroyed. During its progress, information reached the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> that one of the houses, the upper part of which was in flames, contained on the lower basement a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of barrels of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>. A party of seamen had been drafted from the ships in the harbour to assist in arresting the progress of the fire; and these men, with the cool intrepidity which characterizes the sons of the ocean, forced their way into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> premises, and actually succeeded in removing the entire <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of powder, consisting of several thousand pounds in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. A large and handsome church, intended as a monument to the British heroes who fell on the banks of the Sutlej, has been recently built on the island of Colaba, where the cantonments are situated. About a mile N.W. of the fort is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Town. At Bombay the rise of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> has been found sufficient to admit the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of docks on a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. The highest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> tides rise to the height of seventeen feet, and the height of the ordinary tides is fourteen feet. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> advantages, the dry <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCK">dock</a> of Bombay has scarcely its equal for size and convenience; having three divisions, with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of strong gates to each, so that it is capable of receiving three ships of the line at a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Near this dock is a convenient place to heave <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> several ships at once; and this operation is well executed, and with great expedition, by the Parsees, who are generally accounted excellent ship-carpenters. Here is a rope-walk, equal to any in England, with the single exception of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>'s yard at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, where <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> and all sorts of lesser cordage are manufactured. It has also a covering to protect the workmen from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. The dockyard is large and well contrived, having ample supplies of naval stores deposited in the warehouses, together with large quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> for repairing and building ships, and forges for all kinds of smith-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. With these advantages Bombay claims a distinguished <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> as a naval arsenal. Many merchant-ships of from 600 to 1300 tons, partly for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> trade and partly for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the East India <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, have been built in its docks, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of construction, good workmanship, and durability, they have been considered superior to any other class of merchant-ships in the world. Some ships of the line, and several frigates for the British <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, have also been built at this port. Among them may be mentioned the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINDEN">Minden</a>, a 74-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> ship launched in 1810; this was followed some years later by the Wellesley, also a 74-gun ship; and more recently the Mecanee, of 90 guns has been added to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a>. These ships were all built of Mahabar teak, which is esteemed superior to any in India. The teak forests, from which supplies of wood are derived, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> along the western side of the Ghant <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, and other contiguous ridges to the north and east of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BASSEIN">Bassein</a>; the numerous streams which descend from them affording water-carryage for the timber. The docks belong to the Company. They are entirely occupied by Parsees, who are esteemed remarkably skilful and assiduous. Bombay, thus possessing, in the skill of its workmen, the excellence of its timber, and the superiority of its docks, all that is necessary for a naval arsenal, is a station of the first importance to the British power in India. From its position, Bombay commands an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the countries situated in the Persian and Arabian Gulfs. It also possesses much facility of commercial intercourse with different parts of the territories subject to the other presidencies of India, and it carries on a valuable trade with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of export are cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CASHMERE">cashmere</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHAWLS">shawls</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, opium, coffee, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> imports are British <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, raw <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a> from China, wine, beer, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TEA">tea</a>. The foreign trade has more than doubled within the last twenty years; and its exports alone now amount to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> millions <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. The value (in rupees) of the imports and exports to the United <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">Kingdom</a> has increased thus: | Year | Imports | Exports | |--------|---------|---------| | 1813-14 | Rs. 926,980 | Rs. 3,051,543 | | 1823-24 | 5,571,313 | 5,953,859 | | 1833-34 | 9,042,390 | 10,184,735 | | 1843-44 | 24,335,718 | 17,046,748 | | 1852-53 | 29,319,750 | 29,385,955 | The shipping that entered and cleared the port in 1852-53, was as follows: | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYPE">Type</a> | Arrived | Departed | |---------------|---------|----------| | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>-rigged | 522 | 522 | | Country craft | 41,719 | 41,696 | | Total | 42,241 | 42,218 | <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a>. According to the census of 1849 Bombay Island, with Colaba, contains a population of 566,119. This amount is inclusive of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> and also of the floating population of the harbour. More than one-half of the inhabitants are Hindus. The Mahometans somewhat exceed one-fifth of the entire population. Next in point of numbers are the Parsees. Many of this last-mentioned class are extensively engaged in commerce; they are the brokers and factors of Europeans, and share largely in most of the foreign speculations of European mercantile houses. They are a rich, industrious, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> body of men, who contribute greatly to the prosperity of the settlement. The Parsees are the descendants of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fire-worshippers of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, who took refuge in Khorassan upon the conquest of that country by the Moslems in the seventh century. Their first appearance in India occurred about the year 768, and their earliest settlement was the island of Diu, on the south <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the peninsula of Kattwar. From thence they migrated to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROACH">Broach</a>, and finally to Bombay. The various castes into which the total population of Bombay is distributed, and the proportion comprised in each, are thus particularized: | Caste | Number | |-----------------------|--------| | Jains, Lingachs, or Boodhists | 1,902 | | Brahmins | 6,936 | | Hindus of other castes | 259,995 | | Musselmans | 124,153 | | Parsees | 114,698 | | Jews | 1,132 | | Native <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> | 7,456 | | Indo-Britons | 1,333 | | Indo-Portuguese | 5,417 | | Pure European | 5,088 | | Seeede, Negro, African | 889 | | Other castes | 7,118 | | **Total** | **566,119** | It has been often remarked that the people of India differ from Europeans, not only in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and in creed, but also in their manners and modes of thought. A striking illustration of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the observation is afforded in the organization and existence to a very recent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the great plundering confederacy of Bombay. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a>, composed of upwards of forty individuals, and affording employment to between two and three hundred subordinates, had been established upwards of thirty years for the receipt of goods stolen from merchant-ships. The harbour was the principal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of plunder, where the members of the gang were each <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> systematically distributed at the different quays, from which their boats and canoes were sent off to the loading and unloading ships. The plunder obtained was conveyed openly to the shore as though legally acquired, and thence transported to the partnership warehouses, where each morning it was brought to auction without any attempt at concealment. The books were kept with strict regularity, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of profits made with scrupulous honesty; two shares being invariably reserved to be distributed in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. This successful perpetration of offences, though practised without interruption for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years, had been carried on without suspicion on the part of the European officers of the government; while the silence of the natives was secured either by the respect for caste, or by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to intimidation. It was not till the year 1843 that the system was discovered, and those concerned in it brought to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. The Company's naval force at Bombay, including frigates, Naval <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> steamers, and other craft, consists of forty-six vessels, and force to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> this navy a regular establishment of officers and seamen is required. The western coast of India, from the shores of the Persian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> to Goa, was formerly infested by hordes of pirates, who were distinguished, particularly those in the northerly tracts, by courage, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, and habits of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> ferocity. It was to protect the country trade against the depredations of these banditti, who had haunted those seas since the time of Alexander the Great, that the East India Company found it necessary to maintain an armed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> force. The military force of the presidency, composed of the Military regular troops of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a> and Company, but exclusive of local and police corps, amounts to 41,426 men, of whom 10,244 are Europeans, and 31,182 natives. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the strength of the local and police corps be added, the aggregate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be swelled to 59,430. An augmentation of force being required, consequent upon the recent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the British dominions in India, another European regiment is about to be added to the infantry of this presidency. The principal divisions of the Bombay <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> are as follow: | Presidency Garrison—Headquarters, Bombay | European | Native | Total | |------------------------------------------|----------|--------|-------| | Southern Division—Headquarters, Belgaum | 678 | 3,264 | 3,942 | | Poona Division—Headquarters, Poona | 1,399 | 8,117 | 9,516 | | Northern Division—Headquarters, Ahmedabad | 3,736 | 10,729 | 14,465| | Asseerghur fortress | 14 | 573 | 587 | | <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADEN">Aden</a> force | 659 | 1,405 | 2,064 | | Sindh Division—Headquarters, Kurrahees | 2,461 | 12,964 | 15,425| | Rajpootana field force | 181 | 3,757 | 3,938 | | Deduct <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a> troops | 10,504 | 2,637 | 13,141| | Deduct local and police corps | 10,297 | 40,133 | 50,430| | Total regular troops, Crown and Company's | 10,244 | 31,182 | 41,426| <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">Education</a>. A board of instruction presides over the government educational establishments of this presidency. These institutions consist of two principal classes. The first comprehends all the vernacular <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> in which knowledge is communicated through the medium of the native languages. Under the second are ranked the institutions in which the higher branches of learning are taught through the medium of English. Various particulars connected with these seminaries are detailed in the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. | Expense | Teachers | Pupils | |---------|----------|--------| | English and mixed Instruction | | | | Elphinstone Institutions—<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> | 30 | 42 | | Schools (two) | 520 | | Branch schools (two) | 8 | 404 | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRANT">Grant</a> Medical College | 6 | 27 | | Poona school | 2 | 169 | | Ahmednagar school | 1 | 52 | | Sarat school | 9 | 290 | | Ahmedabad school | 2 | 29 | | Broach school | 1 | 67 | | Ruttanaghyerry school | 1 | 51 | | Dharwar school | 2 | 40 | | Poona Sanscrit College | ... | 305 | | Total | 62 | 2,066 | Vernacular Instruction. | No. of Schools | |----------------| | Presidency | 7 | | First Division | 133 | | Second Division | 37 | | Third Division | 56 | | Total | 233 | In 1827 a supreme <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of justice was established at Bombay, constituted under letters-patent from the crown, under powers granted by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It consists of a chief justice and one puisne judge, from whose decision an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> lies to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. The modes of procedure in this court are assimilated to those of the courts at Westminster; but its jurisdiction is restricted to the city of Bombay, except in regard to British subjects. Facilities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>, so important to the prosperity of commerce, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, and manufactures, as well as to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RAILWAYS">railways</a>, essential to social improvements, are for the most part rare in India. In the Bombay territories government has made considerable efforts to effect beneficial changes in this respect, but the difficulties are many, various, and sometimes almost insurmountable. The great expense of constructing <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> of materials calculated for durability, with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a>, bridges, and other appurtenances essential to their completeness, and of maintaining them in a state of efficiency, is but one among those difficulties. Another is the character of the country to be traversed; roads, in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> connecting places of some importance, have in the intermediate space to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through a tract of country little if at all removed from the character of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. A further, and in a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> a peculiar difficulty arises from the frequent deficiency of water. The construction of roads in the hot <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Bombay is useless unless water can be found for the consumption of the beasts of burden, and this has frequently to be provided by additional works, involving an increased outlay. If to these sources of difficulty and expense be added that arising from the rugged and mountainous character of a large part of the country; the feeling likely to be excited will be that of surprise that so much should have been effected. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> obstacle, after leaving the coast, is the range of mountains known as the Western Ghauts, the principal passes in which are at present the Tull and the Bhore Ghaut, traversed by what may be termed two radical roads, connecting the port of Bombay with the interior. A railway from the city of Bombay, traversing the country in a northerly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and intended to effect a junction with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> line, is now under construction, and has been opened as far as Tannah. A branch line from this will connect the cotton districts of the valley of Berar with the port of shipment on the western coast; while another in a south-eastern direction, via Poonah and Bellary, is projected, to facilitate communication with Madras. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. Bombay Island appears to have been first occupied by the Portuguese about the year 1530, having been previously dependent on the ruler of Guzerat. In 1661 it was ceded by the crown of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> in full sovereignty to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the Second of England, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> concluded with that power when he espoused the Infanta; and shortly after it was transferred by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> grant to the East India Company. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time it superseded in importance the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> at Surat, and became the principal British settlement on the western coast. Aurungzebe, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Delhi, invaded the island in 1688 and laid siege to the town, but was prevailed upon to withdraw his troops upon the receipt of a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. The extension of the British dominions on the western side of India was both slow and subject to frequent checks. Previously to the year 1775 the possessions of the East India Company in this quarter of the empire were limited to the island of Bombay, the harbour of Bankote, with Port Victoria, and the factories of Ahmedabad, Broach, and Surat. In the year last-mentioned, Salsette and the adjacent islands were obtained by treaty with the Peishwa. About the same period various acquisitions were made in Guzerat, but these, after a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> occupation by their new masters, again reverted to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a>. It was not till the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the eighteenth century that the company obtained the grant of the city and territory of Surat, nor until the commencement of the nineteenth, that the district of Broach became permanently a British possession. By the treaty of Baroda in 1805, portions of the collectories of Ahmedabad and Kaira were ceded by the Guicowar, as were the ports of Malwan, Vingora, and some others, by the rajas of Kolapore and Sa-wunt Warree. These, however, in the aggregate constitute but a fragment of the territory now comprised within the presidency, the great bulk of which is of still more recent acquisition. One vast accession took place in 1818, upon the downfall of the Peishwa, when the possessions of that potentate were incorporated with the Company's dominions. Since that period the limits of the British empire on the side of Western India have been still further extended by the annexation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SINDE">Sinde</a>, and the transfer to the Company of the Angrias territories, and the principality of Sattara. The first of these became subject to British rule by the results of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>; the latter two lapsed to the paramount power upon the failure of heirs to their last native rulers. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOMB">BOMB</a>-KETCH. See BOMB-VESSEL.

BOMBUS

Pages 14-14

literally, a deep hollow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> humming noise, such as the buzzing of bees. The word was used to denote a kind of applause with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> auditories. (Suet. Nero, 20.) This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> is also employed to designate a genus of insects, of which our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> Humble <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEE">Bee</a> is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYPE">type</a>. See ENTOMOLOGY.

BOMONICE

Pages 14-14

the name given to those Lacedemonian youths who contended at the altar of Artemis Orthia for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of endurance, by submitting their bodies to the lash. (Hyg. Fab. 261.)

BONA

Pages 14-15

a fortified town and seaport of Algiers, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and 85 miles N.E. of the town of Constantine, is situated on an open <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> at the mouth of the Seyhouse in Lat. 36° 54' N. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 47' E. The town is about two miles in circumference, and is surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wall with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> turrets and four gates. It has been much improved since it came into the possession of the French, by the formation of good streets and squares, and the erection of many handsome and commodious houses. It now has bazaars, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, coffee-houses, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-READING">reading</a>-rooms, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, two Roman Catholic chapels, synagogue, mosque, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, and several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>; and it is the seat of a tribunal of primary instance. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> seat of the coral fishery, and has a considerable trade in corn, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, and wax; and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of native garments, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, saddles, &c. The town and harbour are defended by a citadel, Casbah, on a hill a little to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the town, and surrounded by thick walls, about a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in circuit. Remains of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hippo-regius, celebrated as the see of St Augustine, are to be found about a mile to the south of the town, and consist principally of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cisterns, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Roman walls. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Bona in 1850 amounted to 8134, of whom 5250 were Europeans. Bona Dea, a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, who is described as the wife, sister, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Faunus, and so famous for her chastity that after her <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> she was deified. Her sacrifices were performed only by women, and in so secret a manner that it was death for any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> to intrude himself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. Cicero reproaches P. Clodius with having entered this temple disguised as a singing woman, and by his presence polluted the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the Bona Dea. What kind of mysteries these were, we learn incidentally from Juvenal, Sat. vi. 313, where the abominations practised in them are very significantly pointed at. Bona Fides, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. When a person performs any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> which he believes at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> to be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> and lawful, he is said to have acted in bona fide, "in good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>." Bona Mobilia, movable effects or goods. Bona Notabilia are such goods as a person dying has in another <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> than that in which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> dies, amounting to the value of five pounds at least; in which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the deceased must be proved, or administration granted, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the archbishop of the province, unless, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, any dioceses are authorized to do it, when rated at a greater sum. Bona Vacantia, goods, such as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> fish, shipwrecks, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREASURE_TROVE"><a class="xref</a>" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>-trove, waifs, and strays, in which no one can claim a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. BONALD (<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">LOUIS</a> GABRIEL <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBOISE">AMBOISE</a>) VICOMTE DE, a French philosophical writer, was born in the year 1754 at Monna, near Milhan, in the department of Aveyron. He began <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> as a soldier, but having little sympathy with the revolutionary principles then abroad, he emigrated in 1791 and joined the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Condé. Soon afterwards he quitted the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and retired to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a>, where he devoted himself entirely to literature. His first <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled Théorie du Pouvoir Politique et Religieux, was published at Con- Bonaparte stance in 1796, but was interdicted by the French Directory. It was republished at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1843. Though a staunch supporter of the Bourbons, Bonald returned in 1804 to Paris, where he supported himself for many years by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, refusing various advantageous offers from the family of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a>. In 1815 he was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> for Aveyron, and distinguished himself by his efforts to check the abuses of the press. In 1823 he was nominated a peer of France, and accepted office under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; but he lost both his <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by refusing to take oath to the new government of 1830. In that year he retired to his birthplace, where he died on the 23rd November 1840, at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of eighty-six. His philosophical, social, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> theories are based on this proposition, "L'homme pense sa parole, avant de parler sa pensée. Loin que la parole soit le produit de la pensée c'est elle-même qui en est le principe. Or, si la parole est antérieure à la pensée d'où peut elle venir, si non de Dieu même?" The principal works of M. Bonald, besides those already mentioned, are La <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">Legislation</a> Primitive, Paris, 1821, 3 vols. 8vo; Recherches Philosophiques sur les premiers Objets des connaissances morales, 2 vols. 8vo, 1818 and 1826; Démonstration Philosophique du principe constitutif de la Société, Paris, 1830, 8vo.

BONARELLI

Pages 15-15

DELLA ROVESE, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">COUNT</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GUID">GUID</a>' UBALDO, an Italian poet, born at Urbino, A.D. 1563, was the son of Count Pietro Bonarelli, minister of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Urbino. He was intrusted with several important negotiations, and was esteemed an able politician and learned <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. He was the author of a pastoral entitled Filii di Sciro, printed for the first <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> in 1607, with cuts, 4to; and of an amatory production entitled Discorsi in difesa del doppio Amor della sua Celia, first printed at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a> in 1612, 4to. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FANO">Fano</a> in 1608. His <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Prospero and his nephew Pietro were also writers of poems, &c.

BONASONE

Pages 15-15

GIULIO, an admirable engraver, born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> about 1498. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> under Lor. Sabbatini, but attained small proficiency in that branch. The freedom and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, however, of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ETCHING">etching</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> and burin are most excellent; and we owe to him engravings from the works of Michael Angelo, Raphael, Titian, and many other illustrious painters, that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> always hang <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his name as among the most eminent in that department of the arts. BONASSUS. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. BONAVENTURE (Bonaventura) St., one of the brightest luminaries of the scholastic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born of a good family, at Bagarese in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, in 1221. His original name was Giovanni di Fidenza, but from a particular incident in his childhood he received the name by which alone he is now generally known. In 1243 he entered the order of St Francis, and after several years' <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> under the celebrated Alexander of Hales, he was in 1253 appointed to lecture publicly on the Sentences of Lombard. In 1255 he took his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> on the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> with Aquinas. The year following he was chosen general of his order, which he governed till his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> with vigour and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>. He is said to have declined the offer of the see of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a> from Clement IV., in 1265; and might on the death of that pope have been elected in his stead, the cardinals having solemnly engaged themselves to abide by the choice of Bonaventure, even <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he should nominate himself. The person whom he recommended was Theobald, archbishop of Liège, at that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the Holy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">Land</a>. The new pope, who assumed the name of Gregory X., appointed Bonaventure in 1273 to the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBANO">Albano</a>, and soon after raised him to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>. Bonaventure died <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 15, 1274, while attending the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Lyons as legate of the pope. His remains were attended to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> by the pope and the whole council; they were exhumed in the sixteenth century by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a>, burnt, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into the Saône. Bonaventure was canonized in 1482 by Sixtus IV., and ranked in 1587 by Sixtus V. as the sixth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> doctor of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BONAVISTA">Bonavista</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Lyons chose him as her <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> saint. The purity and gentleness of his character, and the heavenly thoughts with which his writings abound, procured him among scholastic divines the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the seraphic doctor. By the Franciscans he is regarded as the greatest doctor of their order, and held up as a rival to St Thomas, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a>. His works, printed at Rome 1588-96, in eight vols. folio, comprise commentaries on the Scriptures and on the Book of Sentences, numerous tracts chiefly on ascetic and practical subjects, sermons, letters, &c. This collection includes several apocryphal works, among which is the famous Psalter of the Virgin. His efforts to make <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> (which with him is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of Peripateticism and Neoplatonism) subservient to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, resulted in a pious mysticism which makes his meaning often obscure. Union with God he regards as the sovereign good, and this principle he has developed in his Itinerarium Mentis in Deum and his Reductio artium in Theologiam. The latter treatise is devoted to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> consummation of all science and art. Bonaventure is distinguished above all the schoolmen by his freedom from trivial subtleties, his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> fervour, and the practical tendency of his spirit. His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on Lombard contains a most acute refutation of the doctrine of the eternity of the world, and some new arguments for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. He is eulogized by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> as an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> (Bonaventura, praestantissimus vir); and characterized by Bellarmine as a doctor alike beloved by God and man.

BONAVISTA

Pages 15-15
or BOAIVSTA, an island near the western coast of Africa, forming part of the group called Cape de Verd, from their vicinity to that remarkable promontory. It was the first of the number discovered by the Portuguese in 1450. Captain Porter describes the island as consisting of a level plain, rising in the centre into rugged and rocky eminences. A great part is capable of cultivation, and might yield in abundance cotton and indigo, were these properly attended to by the indolent natives. Pop. 4395, chiefly engaged in the manufacture of salt. There are three good roads for shipping. The north-west point is in Long. 22° 56' 24" E. and Lat. 16° 13' 18" N.

BOND

Pages 15-15

JOHN, a commentator on Horace and Persius, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> in 1550, educated at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a> school, and at New <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, by which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> he was appointed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the free school at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TAUNTON">Taunton</a>. In this situation he acquired some reputation; but growing weary of teaching he applied to physic, and practised, it is said, with considerable success. He died in 1612. His short marginal annotations upon Horace and Persius (1606 and 1614, 8vo) are generally feeble, and without erudition; yet his edition of the former has often been reprinted. Saxius describes him as minorum gentium philologus.

BONDAGE PROPERLY

Pages 15-15

E properly signifies <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, but in old <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> books it is used for villainage. Tenants in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> paid rentos, did fealty, and were prohibited from felling trees in their own garden, without license of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">lord</a>. The widow of a tenant in bondage held her husband's estate quando exercit sine marito, as <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> as she lived single. Bondage by the Forelock, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Bondagium per anteriorres crines copitis, was when a freeman renounced his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and became a slave to some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, which was done by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off a lock of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> from the forehead, and delivering it to his lord. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he reclaimed his liberty, or became fugitive from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he might be drawn again to his servitude by the nose, whence the origin of the popular menace to pull the nose.

BONDMAN

Pages 15-16

in Old English <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a villain, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> tenant in villainage. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had two kinds of bondmen; one, called servi, who were those either bought for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, taken in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, left by succession, or acquired by some other lawful <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a>; the other, born of their bondwomen, and called We may add a third kind of bondmen mentioned by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, called *adscriptitii glebe*, or *agricensiti*, who were a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of serfs or boors, not bound to the person, but to the ground or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and who followed him who had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>. These in our old law are called *vilains regardants*, as belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> or place.

BONDOU

Pages 16-16

a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Western <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, between 14° and 15° N. Lat., and 11° and 13° W. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is elevated, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are generally unproductive, and covered with stunted wood. The intervening valleys, however, are fertile, and finely clothed with the baobab, the tamarind, and various valuable fruit trees. They are traversed by beds of torrents, which flow rapidly during the rains, but are empty in the dry season. Cultivation, though it extends over only a comparatively small proportion of the whole surface, is carried on with considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. The products consist of four <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grain, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The workmen in the different parts display considerable dexterity, though they employ very rude and defective tools. The people consist chiefly of Foulahs, though the country is much frequented by Mandingoes and Serawoolies for purposes of trade. The exports consist of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and cotton cloth manufactured in the country, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for slaves and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a>, bringing the former from the interior to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> usually through Bondou. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and laws of this country are Mahommedan, though the precepts of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> are not observed with the same rigour as in more northern countries. There are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, however, in every town, where the Koran and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-READING">reading</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of Arabic are taught; but the scholar is treated as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the teacher, for whom he is obliged to perform the most menial offices. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> is nearly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, and commands a considerable body of troops, who are much employed in predatory expeditions, chiefly for the purpose of collecting slaves. His revenues are derived from a tenth <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the produce of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and of the salt imported, as also from duties on goods passing through his territories, with numerous presents expected <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> extorted. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARK">Park</a> experienced to his cost the rapacity of the reigning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, being obliged to give up even the coat which he wore. He was introduced to the king's twelve wives, who had never before seen a European, and thought that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> skin had been produced by his having been bathed in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILK">milk</a> by his mother, who had also artificially pinched up his nose into its unnatural elevation. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence was then at Fatteconda; but when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Gray visited Bondou it had been removed to Boolibani, a small town surrounded by a strong clay wall. The palaces of the king and his sons consist merely of inclosures about an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, containing a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cottages, somewhat larger, but not more commodious, than those of his subjects. **BONE DUST.** See Agricultural <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>.

BONE

Pages 16-16

Henry, R.A.,** the most eminent enamel painter of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRURO">Truro</a> in 1755. He was much employed by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> jewellers for small designs in enamel, before his merits as an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> were well known to the public. In 1800 the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of his pieces attracted the notice of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy, of which he was then admitted as an associate, and in 1811 as an academician. From the beginning of this century until 1831, he executed many beautiful pieces of much larger size than had been attempted before in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: among these his 85 portraits of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, of different sizes, from 5 by 4, to 13 by 8 inches, are most admired. They were disposed of by public <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALE">sale</a> after his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in 1834. His "<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> and Ariadne," after Titian, painted on a plate, brought the great price of 2200 guineas. **<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-BONES">BONES</a>.** See Anatomy and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Boxes of the Dead.** Different usages and ceremonies relating to the bones of the dead have obtained in different ages; as gathering them from the funeral pile, washing, anointing, and depositing them in urns, &c. Among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the bones of travellers and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> dying in foreign countries were brought home to be buried; but during the Italic <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> this was prohibited by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> acknowledged a deity, called *Ossipanga*, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> *Ossipangia*, to whom the care of the induration and knitting of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bones was committed, and who on that account was invoked by pregnant women.

BONET

Pages 16-16
or Bonnet, Theophilus,** an eminent physician, born at Geneva, March 5, 1620. He took his degree in 1643, and then applied himself to the practice of his profession, in which he acquired great reputation. On retiring from practice, he found leisure to collect all the observations he had made during an experience of forty years. But his principal title to distinction is rather as a medical writer than a practitioner, and as having in some measure created pathological anatomy, which Morgagni afterwards illustrated. He died March 29, 1689. His most valuable work is *Splechrectum, sive Anatomia Practica ex cadaveribus morbo denatis*, a valuable mine of morbid anatomy. The best edition is that of Magnetus, Geneva, 3 tom. folio, 1700. His other works are, *Mercurius Compositatus*, Geneva, 1682, fol.; *Zodiacus Medico-Gallicus*; *Medicina Septentrionalis Collatitia*, Geneva, 1684-86, 2 vols. fol.; *Polygones, sive Thesaurus Medico-Practicus*, Geneva, 1690-93, 3 vols. fol.; *Theodori Turqueti de Mayerne Tractatus de Arthritide*, Geneva, 1671, 1674, 12mo, Jacobi Rohaultii Tractatus Physicus*, Geneva, 1674, 8vo, both translations; *Bibliothèque de Médecine et de Chirurgie*, Geneva, 1670, 4 vols.

BONFADIO

Pages 16-16

Jacopo,** a celebrated Italian writer, born at Gazano, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Brescia, about the commencement of the 16th century. He was secretary to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Merinos, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, and afterwards to Cardinal Ghinucci at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>. He read public lectures on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s politics, and on <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, and was appointed professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and historiographer to that republic. He had completed five books of the annals of that state, which were to have been followed by others; but having spoken too freely of some noble families, they resolved upon his ruin, and accused him of an unnatural crime. As witnesses were found to convict him, he was condemned to the flames; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> was commuted, as an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of special <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, into beheading. This took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in 1550. Authors have varied in their opinions as to Bonfadio's alleged guilt; Tiraboschi among others, maintains the affirmative of the question. His works are, 1. *Annationem Genuesium <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> anno 1528 Recuperata Libertatis usque <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> annum 1550, libri quinque*, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, 1586, 4to; 2. *Lettere Famigliari di Jacopo Bonfadio, con altri suoi Composimenti in prosa ed in verso*, with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the author by Mazzucchelli, Brescia, 1746, 8vo.

BONFINI

Pages 16-16

Anthony,** a Latin historian, born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASCOLI">Ascoli</a>, in the marquisate of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1472. His literary fame induced Matthias Hunyadi, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, to invite him to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, where he was retained and pensioned by that sovereign, as well as by his successor Vladislavus. He wrote by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> command the early <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Hungary, which he brought <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the year 1495. It is a well-executed <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and has gone through several editions. Bonfini died in 1502. He has left, 1. *Rerum Ungaricarum decades tres*, Basle, 1545, fol.; 2. *Flavi Philostrati Lemnii Libri ii. de Vitâ Sophistarum*, 1516, 4to; 3. *Hermogenis Libri de Arte Rhetorica et Apothecarii Sophiste Progymnastica*, Lyons, 1538; 4. *In Horatium Flaccum Commentaria*, Rome, without <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, 4to; and, 5. *Symposion Beatricis*, Basle, 1572 and 1621, 8vo.

BONFRERE

Pages 16-16

Janss,** in Latin *Bonferius*, a learned Jesuit, born at Dinand-sur-Meuse in 1573. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, and notes on the Onomasticon, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the places and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> mentioned in Scripture. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOURNAY">Tournay</a> in 1643.

BONGARS

Pages 16-17
or Bongarsius, Jacques,** counsellor and maître d'hôtel to Henri IV., and one of the ablest critics of his time, was born at Orleans in 1546. He studied the belles-lettres at Strasbourg under an anabaptist professor, and law at Bourges under Cajus. He was for about thirty years employed in the most important negotiations of Henri IV. at the courts of the princes of Germany, first as resident, and afterwards as ambassador. Bongars was a Protestant, and happening to be at Rome when Sixtus V. inflamed his famous bull of excommunication against Henri IV., he wrote a spirited answer, which he had the boldness to post up in a conspicuous place, and which was afterwards published with his name in the Mémoires de la Ligue. He died at Paris July 29, 1612. His printed works are, 1. A Collection of the Historians of the Crusades, under the title of Gesta Dei per Francos, Hanau, 1611, fol.; 2. Jacobi Bongarsi Epistolae, Lugd. Bat. 1641; 3. Collectio Hungaricarum Rerum Scriptorum, Francof. 1690, fol.; 4. An edition of Justin, with learned notes; besides notes on Petronius, and various readings of Paulus Diaconus.

BONI

Pages 17-17
or BOSY, a state in the island of Celebes, stretching for part of its extent along the western shores of a great cognominal bay which indents the southern side of the island to the depth of nearly 180 miles. The inhabitants of this once powerful and independent country are the Bugis—a people in many respects the most remarkable of the Eastern Archipelago. Their numbers, by the Dutch census in 1824, amounted to about 200,000. Living, as they do, surrounded by nations notorious for treachery, piracy, and indifference to the arts and objects of civilized life, they have always shown themselves honest, industrious, and ingenious. Agriculture is by them more extensively practised than by any of the adjoining tribes; and of the cotton cloth called cam-bays worn in these regions, they not only manufacture enough for their own use, but also export considerable quantities to the Malay islands. They likewise carry on a considerable traffic in the mineral and vegetable productions of their country, such as gold dust, tortoise-shell, pearls, nutmegs, camphor, and various medicinal preparations; and for these they find a ready market at Singapore, the chief commercial entrepôt of these Eastern seas. In the form and constitution of their government, likewise, they approach more nearly the spirit of true civilization than any other Asiatic people. The highest officer of state is the king or president, who is elected generally for life, and always from their own number, by the chiefs of the eight petty states that compose the nation. His power, however, is so limited that he cannot decide upon any measure of public policy, without the consent of the minor chiefs by whom he was originally appointed. In some of the petty states the office of chief is the hereditary prerogative of a family; in others any member of the privileged classes may aspire to that dignity. Hence it happens not unfrequently that the state comes to be governed by a woman, as the principle of the Salic law is here unknown. Of the history of Boni not much is known. According to Temminck, it first acquired importance in the year 1666, when the rajah Palakkah, whose father and grandfather had been murdered by the family of Hassan the tyrant of Sumatra, made common cause with the Dutch against that despot. From that date till the beginning of the present century the Dutch influence in the polity of the kingdom remained undisputed. In 1814, however, Boni fell into the hands of the British, who retained it for two years; but by the European treaties concluded on the downfall of Napoleon it reverted to its original colonizers.

BONIFACE

Pages 17-17

the name of several eminent men, particularly of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> popes. To the first of these, who was chosen pope in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 418, St Augustin dedicated his four books in answer to the two epistles of the Pelagians.—Boniface II. was elected pope in October 530, and succeeded Felix IV., who had been nominated by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the clergy, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and the people assembled in the basilica of Constantinople, and whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> he caused to be condemned. His pontificate was distinguished only for its turbulence.—Boniface III. was elected in February 606. He prevailed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Phocas to consent that the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Universal Bishop should be conferred on no other but the bishop of Rome, and that the Holy See should have the supremacy over that of Constantinople.—Boniface IV. raised to the papal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in August 608, obtained from the same emperor the Pantheon, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> temple of all the gods, built by Agrippa, and converted it into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which he consecrated to all the martyrs and the Virgin, under the name of Santa <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> della Rotonda.—Boniface V. was elected in December 618, and died in October 624.—Boniface VI. was elected in April 896, but died of the gout fifteen days thereafter.—Boniface VII., called Franco, is styled an antipope. He was suspected of having caused Benedict VI. to be strangled in prison in 974; and after the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of Benedict VII. he removed the treasures of the church to Constantinople. He returned on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Benedict, whose successor John XIV. was disposed of in the same way as Benedict VI. This intruder died in December 985.—Boniface VIII., a pontiff conspicuous for his pretensions to temporal authority, was elected in December 1294. He canonized St <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> in 1297, and in 1300 appointed the jubilee to be solemnized every hundred years thereafter.—Boniface IX. was elected pope on the 2d November 1389, after the death of Urban VI., and during the schism of the west. He supported Ladislaus of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> in his pretensions to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Hungary, against Louis of Anjou, protected by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a> pope, Clement VII. Some writers have praised his moral character; but the greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> have accused him of simony, of cupidity in order to enrich his family, and of exactions for the support of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. He died on the 1st October 1394. Boniface, a saint designated as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APOSTLE">Apostle</a> of Germany, was an Englishman, by name Winifred, and was born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, A.D. 670. He went to preach the gospel among the barbarous nations of Germany; and although created archbishop of Mayence, he soon after resigned his office, in order to preach in East Friesland, where during a tumult he was murdered by the pagans, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 5, 755. With him also perished Eoban a bishop, three priests, three deacons, four monks, and forty-eight laics. The Bollandists collected the Acta Bonifaciana, containing an account of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> of the saint; and a collection of his Letters, amounting to 152, was published by Serrarius in 1605, 4to. In the Speculum of D'Achery may be found the canons which he promulgated for regulating the conduct of his clergy; and one of his sermons is preserved in the Thesaurus Anecdotorum Nocivissim, tom. iii. part 2, published by D. Bernard Pez, at Augsburg, 1729.

BONIFACIO

Pages 17-18

a town in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Corsica, beyond the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, near the strait called Bocca di Bonifacio. It is well fortified, and has a secure harbour, with some trade. Pop. 3120. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 9. 16. E. Lat. 41. 23. 10. N. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BONN">Bonn</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of the circle of the same name in Rhenish <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, is pleasantly situated on the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, 15 miles S.S.E. of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>, with which it is connected by railway. The town has several good streets and a fine market-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. A statue of Beethoven, who was born here on the 17th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1770, was erected, in 1844, in one of the squares. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a fine old edifice in the Byzantine style, surmounted by five towers. Bonn is chiefly celebrated for its university, established by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> of Prussia in 1818, and occupying the extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the electors of Cologne. It has faculties of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, medicine, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, both Protestant and Roman Catholic. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of students in 1849 was 833, of whom 116 were foreigners. It has numbered among its professors Niebuhr and A. W. Schlegel, and among its students, H.R.H. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Albert. The library contains about 150,000 volumes. A beautiful avenue of chestnut trees, about a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length, extends Bonnefons from the university to the chateau of Poppelsdorf, which contains a valuable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and has attached to it a spacious botanic garden. Bonn has one Protestant and three Roman Catholic churches, a synagogue, a gymnasium, and riding-school. Pop. (1849) including the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, 17,688, of whom 14,725 are Catholics. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>; and it has a considerable trade in wine, grain, &c. The circle has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 55,872.

BONNEFONS

Pages 18-18
or BONEFONUS, JERAN, a Latin poet, born at Clermont in Auvergne, A.D. 1554. He studied law under Cujas at Bourges; became an advocate in the parliament of Paris; was appointed lieutenant-general of Bar-sur-Seine; and by his poems acquired great but unmerited reputation, especially by his Pancharis, written in the style of Catullus. He died in 1614. He must not be confounded with John Bonnefons, his son another Latin poet, nor with Dom Elia Benedict Bonnefons, a learned Benedictine of the congregation of St Maur, who died in 1702. The most complete edition of Bonnefons' works is that of Amsterdam, 1767, 12mo, entitled Joannis Bonnefoni patriae Arceani Opera Omnia.

BONNER

Pages 18-18
or BOXER, EDMUND, an English prelate, notorious for his persecutions of the Protestants during the reign of Queen Mary, was born at Hanley in Worcestershire about the end of the fifteenth century, and generally passed for the natural son of George Savage, a priest, who was the natural son of Sir John Savage of Clifton in the same county. Strype, however, says he was positively assured that Bonner was the legitimate offspring of a poor man, who lived in a cottage long afterwards known by the name of Bonner's Place. About the year 1512 he entered as a student of Broadgate Hall (now Pembroke College), Oxford; and in 1519 was admitted as bachelor of the canon and of the civil law. Having been admitted into orders, he obtained some preferment in the diocese of Worcester. In 1525 he took his degree as doctor; and having attracted the notice of Wolsey, that prelate took him under his patronage. Bonner was with the cardinal at Ca'wood when he was arrested on a charge of high treason. After the death of Wolsey he saw his way towards adopting Lutheran sentiments, and found means to insinuate himself into the favour of Henry VIII., who made him one of his chaplains, and employed him in several embassies abroad. In 1532 he was sent to Rome with Sir Edward Carne, to answer for the king, who had been cited to appear in person or by proxy. In 1533 he was again despatched to Pope Clement VII., then at Marseilles, to intimate Henry's appeal to a future general council from the sentence which had been pronounced against his divorce. On this occasion he threatened the pope with so much resolution, that His Holiness talked of having him burned alive or thrown into a cauldron of melted lead. Bonner accordingly judged it prudent to decamp without the ceremony of taking leave. His Holiness did not foresee that the man whom he had thus menaced with the flames was destined to burn heretics in England in support of the very faith which, under Henry, he had lent his aid to overthrow. In 1538, being then ambassador at the court of France, he was nominated bishop of Hereford; but, before consecration, he was translated to the see of London, and enthroned in April 1540. Henry VIII. died in 1547; at which time Bonner was ambassador at the court of the emperor Charles V. During this reign he was constantly zealous in his opposition to the pope; and, in compliance with the king, favoured the Reformation. Henry VIII. was a man to exact a rigid compliance with all his whims and caprices; but on the accession of young Edward, Bonner refused to take the oath of supremacy, and was committed to the Fleet, where he remained until he thought fit to promise obedience to the laws. After his release he continued to comply with the Reformation, but with such manifest neglect and reluctance, that he was twice reprimanded by the privy council, and in 1549 was, after a long trial, committed to the Marshalsea, and deprived of his bishopric. The succeeding reign, however, gave him ample opportunity of revenge.
