The following is the number of persons returned as booksellers and publishers in England and Scotland at the census of 1851: | | Males | Females | Persons | |----------------|-------|---------|---------| | England and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> | 6047 | 858 | 6905 | | Scotland | 1434 | 52 | 1486 | | Total | 7481 | 910 | 8391 | In <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, from the calculation of an extensive bookseller in Dublin, the numbers are as follow: - Booksellers and publishers in Dublin: 40 - Shops for small periodicals in do.: 20 - In the other towns of Ireland: 108 The editor of the Publishers' Circular says, that after careful calculation he finds that "the issues of new publications and new editions are now averaging together 4380 volumes per annum, which, after making full allowance for the improvements in our system of registration, shows an annual issue of nearly one-fourth over that of ten years back. This conclusion is drawn from a pretty safe <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, that of four years, thus: | Year | New books | New editions | |------|-----------|-------------| | 1839 | 2302 | 773 | | 1840 | 2091 | 821 | | 1841 | 2011 | 741 | | 1842 | 2193 | 684 | | 1839-42 | 8397 | 3019 | | Total | 11,616 | | "This does not include pamphlets, of which we have only taken the record during the last three years:—In 1850, there were 1198; in 1851, 940; and in 1852, 908; the noticeable excess for the first year arising from the pamphlet-writing on the Papal question, upon which there were no less than 180 published during one month." The book trade of France is carried on much in the same way as in England. From the last number of the Journal de l'Imprimerie for 1851 we gather the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STATISTICS">statistics</a> of the productions of the French printing-houses during the last ten years: | Year | New books | New editions | |------|-----------|-------------| | 1842 | 6,445 | 1,848 | | 1843 | 6,009 | 1,849 | | 1844 | 6,477 | 1,850 | | 1845 | 6,521 | 1,851 | | 1846 | 5,516 | | | 1847 | 5,590 | | | Total | 64,568 | | or an average per year of 6496 works. The same presses printed, in 1851, 485 musical works, and in the ten years 3336, or an annual average of 333. There have also been published 1014 engravings and lithographs, and during the ten years 13,085, or an average of 1308. Two hundred and fifty-three maps and topographical plans have also been published during the year; during the ten years 1005, or a mean of 100 a year. Thus it appears that nearly in every department of press-work the year 1851 is in advance of the average of the last ten years. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> total of works published in France during these ten years, engravings, musical works, maps, and plans, is 81,994. The bookselling and publishing trade in Germany is differently organized from that of either England or France, and, upon the whole, is carried on by a class of persons of superior intelligence. The principal booksellers of Russia, Holland, Italy, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, are Germans or their descendants. In Germany there is a much larger number of publishers than in any other country of the same size, and they are not, as in Great Britain or France, confined to a few of the principal towns, but are scattered about over the whole country, though, of course, their chief sales are in the numerous small capitals and university towns. The German publishers generally, owing to the small cost of paper and print compared with the expense in England or France, and the comparatively small remuneration to the author, realize, if they sell the whole of an edition, a much larger percentage of profits; but owing to the system there prevailing of sending almost all their works in the first year on sale to the different parts of the country, they are generally obliged, in order to give a book a fair chance, to print a much larger edition than there is any immediate prospect of selling. On the other hand, by this means of making known new books, very little is expended in advertising. There are no wholesale booksellers in Germany, as the term is understood in England and France, the publishers being generally in direct <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with all the principal retail booksellers in every town on the Continent, many of them keeping as many as 1000 to 1500 trade accounts open. But every retail bookseller has his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> or "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>" at Leipzig, and sometimes in other towns in the south of Germany, to whom all parcels for him are sent and forwarded in one package once or twice a-week. This agent also acts as his banker with the trade, almost all payments being made at Leipzig from one agent to another, their weekly or bi-weekly settlements being carried on in a small way on the plan of the clearing-house of the London bankers. At Easter, however, when the general balances of all the booksellers connected with the German trade are made and paid on the booksellers' exchange at Leipzig, the sums are very considerable. Owing to the facility with which the trade of publishing can be carried on in Germany, the absence of all difficulty in immediate communication with the whole retail trade creates a much larger number of publishers in proportion to the number of books published than elsewhere; in fact, almost every bookseller is a publisher to some extent. Nevertheless, the principal publications are in the hands of a limited number of publishers in the strict <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word; and, to some extent, they confine themselves to particular classes of publications. In the United States of America the business of bookselling is carried on to a large extent, principally in books reprinted from English copyright works. These being produced at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> cost of paper and printing, the authors deriving no benefit from their writings, the American ¹ In this case authors should keep in mind that they are, as far as the publication in question is concerned, copartners with the bookseller, and in case of the bankruptcy of the bookseller they are liable for all debts against the book. booksellers are enabled to sell at prices greatly below those of the English market. Of late years, however, they have published many valuable original works, chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, law, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. The publisher of Norton's Literary Gazette estimates the number of volumes published in the United States from July 1850 to July 1851 at 1298, embracing 213,049 pages, and forming 1176 distinct works. The principal towns in which the bookselling business is carried on in the United States are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a>, in which there are 78 booksellers and publishers; New York, in which there are about 130; and Philadelphia, in which there are about 120. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BALTIMORE">Baltimore</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINCINNATI">Cincinnati</a>, St <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>, as well as in all the considerable towns throughout the United States, some books are published; and everywhere there are retailers of school and miscellaneous books. Repeated attempts have been made to induce the American legislature to sanction an international copyright law. Committees of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> have reported in favour of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, but the lower house, composed of the representatives of the people, have constantly resisted it: nor is it likely they will agree to a measure, though <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> in itself, which would prevent their constituents from appropriating the productions of British authors at a greatly reduced price, and which might at the same time diminish the trade of paper-makers, printers, bookbinders, and all engaged in the manufacture of books. (See Copyright.) From the low price at which the reprints of popular English books can be produced, the sale is often four or five times greater than in Britain. It is calculated that 125,000 copies of Macaulay's "England" were sold in America, when scarcely a fifth of that number were sold in Britain. The profit of these, at the selling price of 32s. or $8, would amount to $1,000,000, but as they were supplied at 80 cents, the profits amounted to only 100,000. In this case there is no remuneration to the author, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYPE">type</a> is small, and the paper thin and inferior; and as a large sale can be calculated on with certainty, very large editions are thrown off by machinery, so that the cost is reduced to little more than that of the paper. "But it will be asked," says Mr Carey, "is it <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> that we should read the works of Macaulay, Dickens, and others, without compensation to the authors?" In answer it may be said that we give them precisely what their own countrymen have given to their Dalton, Davy, Parry, and the thousands of others who have furnished the bodies of which books are composed, and more than we ourselves give to the men among us engaged in cultivating science—fame." Authors have often had but scanty fare, but if they were confined to Mr Carey's luxuries their condition would hardly be improved. Mr Carey informs us that there have been sold in the United States in five years 80,000 volumes of the 8vo edition of the Modern British Essayists; of Macaulay's Miscellanies, in 3 vols. 12mo, 60,000 volumes; of Miss <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGUILAR">Aguilar</a>'s writings, 100,000 volumes in two years; of Murray's Encyclopedia of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, more than 50,000; McCulloch's Commercial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, 10,000; of Alexander Smith's poems, in a few months, 10,000. The sale of Thackeray's works has been quadruple that of England, and that of Dickens' works counts by millions of volumes. Bleak House alone sold to the amount of 250,000 in volumes, magazines, and newspapers. Bulwer's last work reached about two-thirds of that number; Alison's Europe 25,000 copies; of Jane Eyre there have been sold 80,000. The universality of education in the United States is the main cause of an extensive publication of books. Everybody must learn to read and write, and everybody must have books; hence the great circulation, not only of foreign but of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> literature. The sale of many of their more popular works, especially of educational publications, is prodigious: 1 Letters on International Copyright, by H. C. Carey, author of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">Political</a> Economy, &c. Philadelphia, 1853. and is glad at the end of three or four years, if, besides the loss of interest of money, he has not a large proportion of the edition lying on his hands as waste paper. In 1852 the booksellers of London formed a kind of trade-union, by which they attempted to exclude from the trade all who would not keep up their prices to what was called the regular rate. This, like all associations of the kind, soon fell to pieces, and various plans were proposed by which the readers might be furnished with books at a smaller deduction from the cost of production. It has not, however, been found possible to dispense with the machinery by which the productions of the press can be distributed through the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of readers; and this convenient machinery must be paid for till one less costly be discovered which will accomplish its objects as well.

BOOMERANG

Pages 43-43

a missile <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of the Australian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABORIGINES">aborigines</a>, with which they are said to be very dexterous in hitting birds. It consists of a piece of hard wood, with the curve of a parabola, and is about 2 feet <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, 2½ inches <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, ½ inch thick, and rounded at the extremities. One side is flat, the other is rounded, and it is brought to a bluntish edge. It is discharged with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> by one end, the convex edge being forward and the flat side upwards. After advancing some distance, and ascending slowly in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> with a quick rotary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, it begins to retrograde, and finally falls to the ground behind the projector. The principle of the boomerang has been attempted to be applied to the propulsion of ships. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STEAM">Steam</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>.

BOOMING

Pages 43-43

among sailors, denotes the application of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BOOM">boom</a> to the sails, in order to accelerate the speed of the ship.

BOONDEE

Pages 43-43

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Rajpootana, situated on the southern declivity of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> range of hills which run nearly from east to west. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the raja is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and was intended to serve as a fortress, though it would not be long tenable against <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TACTICS">tactics</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. The territory of which this town is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> contains an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 2291 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> estimated at 230,000; and the revenues of the raja are returned at L50,000 per annum. During the progress of the Piedarrie and Mahratta <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> had espoused the cause of the British, and shown himself a warm supporter of their views; and upon its termination in 1818, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> was concluded between the two governments, containing the usual stipulations of friendship and protection on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the paramount power, and of subordinate co-operation on the part of the allied state. Boondee is distant from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, southwest, 245 miles. Lat. 25° 26'. Long. 75° 43'.

BOORHANPOOR

Pages 43-43

a decayed town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the territory of Gwalior, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> possessions of the Mahratta family of Scindia, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Taptee. It was formerly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and flourishing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, being the seat of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the kings of Candesh, one of whom, Malik Nasir, founded it in the year 1414. Akbar, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, annexed it with the adjacent territory to the imperial dominions in 1599; and during the reign of his son Jehangir it was visited by the English <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> Sir Thomas Roe, on his route from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a> to the Mogul <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. In the early <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the last century it was wrested from the empire by the Nizam of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HYDERABAD">Hyderabad</a>, and at a later <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> became the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of Madhajee Scindia in his rapid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of conquest. During the Mahratta <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 1803 it was occupied by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Stevenson's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> without opposition, but restored at the conclusion of the peace in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> following. Distance from Oojin 132 miles; from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a> 280. Lat. 21° 18'. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76° 20'.

BOORO

Pages 43-43

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Asiatic Archipelago, situated between Lat. 3° and 4° S. and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 126° and 127° E. It is of an oval shape, and may be estimated at seventy-five miles in length by thirty-eight in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> breadth. This island is fruitful, producing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, sago, oranges, lemons, citrons, cocoa-nuts, bananas, and pine-apples; also the caipet tree, from the leaves of which the caipet <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is procured. Fine <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> grows on this island, and many kinds of beautiful wood, fit for inlaying; besides <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> ebony, and the palm and the teak trees. Ships may be supplied here with rice, cattle, and other refreshments; and the woods abound with wild boars, goats, and deer, and, among the latter, the babyrusa, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> true <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>-deer, as its name implies. The natives consist of two races, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABORIGINES">aborigines</a>, who live in the interior of the island among inaccessible <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and of whom little is known; and the Moors or Mahometans, who inhabit the northern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and acknowledge the authority of the Dutch. The Chinese trade here for cabinet woods and different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of dye-woods. At Cajelli <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> on its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side there is good anchorage, and at the east end is a Dutch station.

BOOROOJIRD

Pages 43-43

a flourishing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a>, situated at the foot of a mountain. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of a district peopled by a tribe called Lack, who seldom wander far from the spots to which they are partial, but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in villages, and employ themselves in the improvement of their estates. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a>, 12,000.

BOOT

Pages 43-45

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> for the foot and leg. Boots seem to have derived their name from their resemblance to a sort of jacks <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> leathern bottles formerly in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, called botas in Latin, and in the old French boute. Boor, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of torture, by which the leg was squeezed with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> violence, for the purpose of extorting confession. (See Wodrow's Hist. of the Sufferings of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> of Scotland.) **BOOTAN**. This extensive region is situated between Bound-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIBET">Tibet</a>, and between the 26th and 29th degrees aries. of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. To the north it is separated from Tibet by the eastern ridges of the Himalaya range; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSAM">Assam</a> and Goalpara, with the native state of Cooch Behar, form its boundaries to the south; on the east it is bordered by a tract inhabited by uncivilized mountain tribes; and on the west by the native state of Sikkim. Its length from east to west is 230 miles, its breadth 120, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> contained within its limits falls little short of 20,000 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. A slip of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> varying from ten to twenty miles in breadth extends along the base of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> from east to west, and separates the hill-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Bootan from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bengal. With the exception of this narrow tract, the whole of Bootan presents a succession of lofty and rugged Aspect. mountains, abounding in the most picturesque and sublime scenery. "The prospects," says <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Turner, "between abrupt and lofty prominences were inconceivably <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>; hills clothed to their very summits with trees, dark and deep glens, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tops of mountains lost in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, constituted altogether a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of extraordinary magnificence and sublimity." As might be expected from the physical structure and elevation of this alpine region, numerous <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are sent forth in a southerly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, which, forcing their passage through narrow defiles, and precipitated in tremendous cata- racts over frightful precipices, eventually pour their tributary streams into the Brahmapootra. One <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a> is mentioned by Turner as issuing from the high grounds in a collected body, but as descending from so great a height that before it reaches the thick <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> below it is nearly dissipated, and appears like the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> arising from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Of the rivers traversing Bootan, the most considerable is the Momas, which in its progress to the Brahmapootra flows under the walls of Tassigong, beyond which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it is unfordable. At the foot of Tassigong Hill it is crossed by a suspension <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. The other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rivers are the Matchoo, the Thinchinchoo, the Toorsha, the Manchee, and the Durla. The more southern portions of the plains of Bootan bordering upon Bengal are under <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">rice</a> cultivation. Between the cultivated tracts and the mountains occurs an intervening space covered with the most luxuriant vegetation, but pervaded by an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> so deleterious to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> that even those most insured to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> rarely <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through it with impunity. In the hilly <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the country the climate varies according to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of elevation. At the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the inhabitants of Punakha (the winter residence of the rajah) are afraid of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> themselves to an almost vertical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, those of Ghasa <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> all the rigours of winter, and are chilled by perpetual snows; yet both these places are within sight of each other. On the elevated mountain heights it is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and moist, and here the clouds are intercepted and descend in rains. The rains, however, in the vicinity of Tassidundon, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, are moderate. There are frequent showers, but nothing that can be compared to the tropical rains of Bengal. Owing to the great elevation and steepness of the mountains, dreadful tempests of winds arise among the hollows, which are often attended with fatal effects. A considerable village, situated on the brow of a lofty hill, was nearly destroyed by one of these tempests. In one night a hurricane swept <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> houses with their unfortunate inmates <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the steep; and though search was afterwards made, not the slightest trace of them was ever found. Three houses remained; and their tenants, unmoved by the dismal fate of their neighbours, still retained their occupation. The people are industrious, and devote themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, but from the geological structure and physical aspect of the country, the pursuits of husbandry, except in the plains, which are under rice cultivation, are limited to comparatively few spots. In the vicinity of the cottages which are interspersed throughout the mountains, the land is cleared for cultivation, and produces thriving crops of barley, wheat, buckwheat, and others of less importance. Turnips of excellent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> are extensively grown; they are free from fibres, and remarkably sweet. The climate is generally well adapted to the production both of European and Asiatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and vegetables. Potatoes have been introduced, but the cultivation of this valuable root has not been attended with success. The forests abound in a variety of stately trees. Among them are the beech, ash, birch, maple, cypress, and yew; firs and pines cover the mountain heights; and below these, but still at an elevation of eight or nine thousand feet, is a zone of vegetation consisting principally of oaks and rhododendrons. Among these mountains, in the vicinity of Marichong, grows the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> tree. Some of the roots and branches were examined by Turner in the course of his journey to Tibet; but the plant being neither in blossom nor <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> fruit, it was impossible to decide whether it was the true cinnamon or an inferior kind of cassia. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, however, corresponded with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> given of the true cinnamon by Linnaeus. Notwithstanding the great diversity of climate, the uninclosed character of the country, and the difficult fastnesses in which it abounds, there is no great variety nor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of wild animals. Thickets of dense vegetation extend along the base of the mountains, and afford shelter to the elephant, tiger, buffalo, and deer. But in the hills of Bootan wild animals are extremely rare; and Turner mentions, as an extraordinary circumstance, that he one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a multitude of monkeys playing their gambols by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROAD">road</a> side. They are of a tall and handsome kind, with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> faces surrounded by a streak of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and have very <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> slender <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>. They are held sacred by the Bootans as well as by the Hindus. The only <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animal of which is indigenous to Bootan, and is used as a domestic animal, is called tangun, from Tangustan, the general appellation of that assemblage of mountains which constitutes the territory of Bootan. It is peculiar to this tract, not being found in any of the neighbouring countries of Assam, Nepal, Tibet, or Bengal, and unites in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the two qualities of strength and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, being remarkable for symmetry and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> proportions. The Tangun <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> is usually about thirteen <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> high, short-bodied, clean-limbed, and deep in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, yet extremely <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>. Being constantly accustomed to struggle against acclivities, there is a surprising energy and vigour in all his movements; and this indomitable spirit is supposed by Europeans to proceed from a headstrong and ungovernable temper, while in reality it is only an excess of eagerness in the performance of any allotted task. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of this horse usually inclines to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, although those of one colour are rarely to be found. The Bootans are not a warlike people, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> resources of the country are altogether on an insignificant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. Beyond the guards necessary for the defence of the various castles, there is nothing like a standing military force in the country. An insuperable difficulty to the maintenance of such a force would, indeed, be presented in the inadequacy of supplies, and the great distance from which they must be drawn. In so barren and rude a country the manufacturing industry of its people must necessarily be at a low ebb, and the few <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> produced are all destined for home consumption. They consist of coarse blankets and cotton clothes, made by the villagers inhabiting the southern tract bordering upon British territory. Leather, from the hide of the buffalo, imperfectly tanned, is principally used for the soles of snow-boots. Circular bowls are neatly turned from various woods. A small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> is made from the plant described as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAPHNE">Daphne</a> papryfera; and, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> to these be added the straight <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> worn by the men, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> spear and arrowheads, and a few <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> caldrons fabricated from the metal obtained in the country, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of Bootan may be considered nearly complete. The inhabitants of this elevated tract are of active habits and of a herculean make, many of them being six feet high, and are entirely different from the feeble and timid natives of Bengal. A general resemblance of features pervades the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a> of these hardy mountaineers. They are fairer than their Bengal neighbours, and have generally broader faces, with high cheek-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. They have invariably black hair, which it is their fashion to cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the head. The eye, which is a remarkable feature in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a>, is small and black, with long pointed corners, as if stretched and extended by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> means. Their eye-lashes are so thin as to be scarcely perceptible. Their face is rather flat, narrowing from the cheekbones to the chin, and broadest below the eyes,—a physiognomy which somewhat resembles that of the Tartars, though it is far more strongly marked among the Chinese. They have very small beards, and generally reach an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> before they have the appearance of any; in this also resembling the Tartars. They are social and cheerful in their manners. The women and the men mix freely together; and they are frequently seen sitting under the cavities of the rocks or other sheltered places, chatting together in great good humour, and occasionally indulging in obstreperous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>. They generally exhibit a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of rosy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; the women in particular, with their jet black hair, and clear, brisk, black eyes, are a rudeness which, according to Turner, the most florid English rustic would in vain attempt to rival. Yet they are far from being cleanly in their habits; nor are their manners and amusements of a refined <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of living is simple; their food consisting of fruits, vegetables, and roots. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TEA">Tea</a> is as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> a refreshment as in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, but the mode of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> is by an admixture of water, flour, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. A spirit is extracted from rice, wheat, barley, and other grains. The supreme ruler of Bootan is called the Deb Raja. He resides at Tassidundon, and possesses unlimited sway over his subjects. The people follow the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Buddha; and the priests form a distinct class, and are bound by the most rigid vows of celibacy. They are dispersed throughout the country in monasteries, and other buildings appropriated to their use. The Deb Raja has always manifested the strongest inclination to extend his territories by encroaching on those of his neighbours. In 1772 he suddenly invaded the principality of Cooch Behar, a dependency of Bengal; but its rajah having applied to the British for aid, a force under Captain Jones was despatched to Cooch Behar, by means of which the invaders were expelled and pursued into their own territories. Upon meeting with these reverses, the Booteans implored the assistance of the Tibetan authorities; in compliance with the request of the Teshoo <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LAMA">Lama</a>, then regent of Tibet, a cessation of hostilities ensued, and in 1774 a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace was concluded between the East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> and the ruler of Bootan. In 1783 Captain Turner was deputed to Bootan, with a view of promoting commercial intercourse, but his mission was not regarded as successful. From this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> little intercourse took place with Bootan, until the occupation of Assam by the British in 1826. It was then discovered that the Booteans had usurped several tracts of low land lying at the foot of the mountains, called dooras or passes, and for these they then agreed to pay a small tribute; but failing in their obligations, and availing themselves of the command of the passes to commit depredations in the British territories, Captain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBERTON">Pemberton</a> arrived in Bootan in 1837, commissioned to adjust the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of difference. His negotiation was productive of no definite result; and every other means of obtaining redress and security proving unsuccessful, the dooras were wrested from the Booteans, and placed under British management. (v. t.)

BOOTES

Pages 45-45

a constellation of the northern hemisphere. It contains Arcturus, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the first magnitude.

BOOTH

Pages 45-45

Barton**, a celebrated English tragedian, born of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, in 1681. He was educated in Westminster school under the celebrated Dr Bushby, where his success in the Latin plays customarily performed by the scholars gave him an inclination for the stage. He was intended for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but at seventeen years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> he ran away from school, and joined a theatrical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. His first appearance was hailed with applause; and from this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> daily improving. After two successful campaigns in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> he returned to his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, having first reconciled himself to his friends. Betterton, to whom he had an introduction, received him with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cordiality, and gave him all the assistance in his power. His success at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> was complete, and he established his reputation as only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> to his great instructor. He was indebted to a happy coincidence of merit and chance for that height of fame which he at length attained in the character of Cato. The Whigs, in favour of whose principles this tragedy was apparently written, thought it their duty to support it strongly; while the Tories, at every passage susceptible of a popular turn, were no less vehement in their approbation. Booth was twice married; first to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir William Barkham, Bart., and afterwards to Miss Hester Santlow, an actress of great merit. During the twenty years of his management, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> was in the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>; and his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened on the 10th of May 1735, contributed not a little to its decline. Booth was a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> of excellent character, and greatly esteemed for his amiability and goodness of heart.

BOOTHIA FELIX

Pages 45-45

an extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of British <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, between Lat. 69. and 75. N. and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 92. and 97. W. It was discovered by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a>, now Sir J. Ross, in 1830; and named after Sir Felix Booth. It forms the western side of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of the same name, into which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Regent's Inlet leads from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAFFIN_S_BAY">Baffin's <a </a>class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>. It is almost separated from the American shores by a chain of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>; and is perhaps joined to North Somerset, discovered by Sir E. Parry in 1819.

BOOTON

Pages 45-45

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Eastern Archipelago, situated off the south-eastern extremity of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CELEBES">Celebes</a>, about the 5th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of south latitude. It is estimated at eighty-five miles in length by twenty miles in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> breadth. It is separated from the island of Angaonai by a narrow strait; and is productive, yielding <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, maize, yams, and a variety of tropical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The inhabitants are of a short stature and tawny <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. They speak the Malay <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and are Mahometans. The Dutch had formerly a settlement here in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Booton.

BOPAL

Pages 45-45

an extensive town of Hindostan, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Malwa, surrounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> wall, on the outside of which is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> gurje <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> mart, with wide and straight streets. On a rising ground to the S.W. of the town is a fort called Futtehgar, built on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock, and surrounded with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> towers. Under the walls of the fort is a tank or lake four miles and a half in length. The territory of which this town is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> contains an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 6764 square miles, and belongs to a native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, whose revenues amount to L220,000 per annum. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> relations of the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> with this state commenced in 1818, when a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> was concluded, the leading <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of which are of the usual character—protection by the British government, and acknowledgment of its supremacy by that of Bopal, with a stipulation for subordinate co-operation. The state of Bopal boasts of no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. Its founder, Dost Mahomed Khan, exercised subordinate authority within its limits, under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Aurungzebe, at the commencement of the eighteenth century; and, upon the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> he assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Nawabu. Subsequently Bopal attracted some notice; first, in 1778, from the circumstance of its ruler rendering assistance to a British force under General Goddard, which traversed a large <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> through states then, with the exception of Bopal, all unfriendly; and again, in 1813, when the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Bopal sustained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months' siege from a combined Mahratta force amounting to at least six times the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the garrison, by whom the assailants were ultimately compelled to abandon their attempt. The Nawabu, with whom the British treaty of 1818 was concluded, died shortly afterwards from the effect of an accidental pistol <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, and was succeeded by an infant nephew, between whom and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the deceased prince, also of tender <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> was negotiated. When, however, the age of the young prince entitled him to look for admission to actual power, his claim was opposed by the Begum, widow of the deceased Nawabu, a woman of some ability, and who had enjoyed since the death of her husband a large share of influence and authority. She disputed not only his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the throne, but also the claim founded on his betrothal to the infant heiress, and he was obliged to relinquish both in favour of a younger <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, who, however, when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> came for asserting his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, received similar treatment from the Begum, who was resolved to retain her position at the head of the state as <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> as possible. The prince's marriage at length took place, but sovereignty was still withheld, and would have been withheld so long as the Begum lived, had not arms achieved what negotiation was unable to accomplish. The new ruler did not long survive his recognition, and as his daughter, a child only six years old, was his successor, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> enforced the re-establishment of a regency, in which the Begum managed finally to gratify her ambition and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of intrigue by attaining a chief part. Such is the present state of affairs in Bopal, where he who shall be so fortunate as to secure the person of the youthful princess in marriage <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> hereafter wield the sceptre of authority.

BORACIC ACID

Pages 45-46

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, the only known <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of boron and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a>, occurs in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> pearly scales, which are soft and greasy to the touch, and have an acidulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. It fuses easily in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, and yields a glossy globule, which on cooling becomes opaque <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any gypsum be in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>. When dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a> it communicates to the flame a fine green tinge; a test which affords the best possible indication of the presence of boric acid. Its specific gravity is equal to 1.48; and, according to Berzelius, it consists of boron 25.83, and oxygen 74.17. The most celebrated deposit of this substance is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLFATARA">Solfatara</a>, within the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRATER">crater</a> of Volcano, one of the Lipari isles, where it is sublimated in the form of a thin filament <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> cake on the surface of the sulphur and around the fumaroles, whence it arises. These incrustations are usually about an inch in thickness, have sometimes a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> structure, and are always more or less tinged with sulphur. It occurs both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> and pulverulent; in which last <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> the particles form merely a filament or loose covering on the surface of the sulphur, without any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a> to each other. Boracic acid is likewise deposited by several of the lagunes in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and at the hot <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of Sasso, a locality which has procured it the trivial name of Sassoline. The mineral from these deposits, however, differs materially in appearance from that of Volcano. It is grayer in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, considerably harder, and shows traces of indistinct <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>. Klaproth found that the Tuscan variety contains eleven per cent. sulphate of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>, an ingredient totally foreign to that from Volcano.

BORAK

Pages 46-46

a fabulous animal, on which Mahomet was supposed to have been carried in his nocturnal flight from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> to heaven.

BORASSUS

Pages 46-46

a genus of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of Palms. The best known is B. flabelliformis <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Toddy-palm, which in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> yields a vinous juice and much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. This palm is 20 feet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, the leaves 4 feet <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> on foot-stalks of the same length. The juice is obtained by crushing the inflorescence, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the upper <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, and fastening the lower part to a vessel of bamboo, into which it <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a>. The fruit has the bigness of a small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> head. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>.

BORAX

Pages 46-46

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>: borate of soda, tinkel, soude boratique. This <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> is usually of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> grey <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, translucent, feebly alkaline to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, soluble in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and consists, according to Klaproth, of soda 14.5, boracic acid 37.0, and water 47.0. It intumesces before the blow-pipe, and then melts into a transparent globule; when in solution it changes the blue colour of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LITMUS">litmus</a> into green. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> locality is <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIBET">Tibet</a>, where it is found on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, in the vicinity and at the bottom of certain <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. It is there collected and sent to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> in the form of a brownish-gray impure salt, from which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> borax is obtained by the addition of a greater <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of soda. It is made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of as a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLUX">flux</a>, in forming <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> gems, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of soldering. It is also of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> utility in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> by the blow-pipe, and in some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in glass manufactories. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> and Mineralogy.

BORDA

Pages 46-48

John <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, a mathematician and nautical astronomer, celebrated for his improvements in the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HYDRAULICS">hydraulics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PNEUMATICS">pneumatics</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of instruments for observation. He was born at Drax, on the 4th of May 1733, and was originally destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; but abandoned the pursuit of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> in favour of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, which he considered as better calculated to afford him opportunities for the cultivation of his mathematical talents, and for the application of the results of his studies to practice. His acquirements in science had very early attracted the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of D'Alembert, who predicted his future eminence, and warmly recommended his <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> his thoughts to the occupation of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the academy. He obtained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> cavalry, and was appointed teacher of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> to the corps; and, in 1756, he presented to the Academy of Sciences (A) A Memoir on the Paths of Bombs, which was ordered to be printed in the collection of the Sciences Étrangères, but which has not excited much attention. He was elected in the same year a member of the academy; and in the next he was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Hastinbeck, in the capacity of aid-de-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> to the celebrated General Maillebois, to whom he looked up as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He was afterwards admitted into the corps of engineers, without the usual form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> into his qualifications; and being stationed at a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port, the occurrences of the place naturally directed his attention anew to the phenomena of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESISTANCE_OF_FLUIDS">resistance of <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>. He published, in 1763, a detailed memoir on this subject (B. Mem. Ac. Par. 1763, p. 338), in which he relates a variety of experiments, showing that the resistance of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> is actually <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the velocity, as had <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> been supposed from theoretical considerations. He also determines, by other experiments, the magnitude of the resistance to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a sphere, and proves that nothing can be more erroneous than the supposition that the resistance to an oblique surface decreases as the square of the sine of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INCIDENCE">incidence</a>. He also finds, that the resistance to the motion of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a>, in the directions of the diagonal of its base and of one of the sides, are as 21 to 16, while the calculations of former theorists had made the resistance greatest in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the side. In 1766 he published an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the discharge of fluids through the orifices of vessels (C. Mem. Ac. Par. 1766, p. 579), in which he first states the objections to considering the different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of a fluid as descending in all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> very nearly in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> directions; he examines the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the jet after its escape from the orifice, and determines some of the effects of abrupt changes in the velocity of the fluid passing through <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> apertures of different forms. He contributed, in 1767, to the publications of the academy, an important Memoir on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">Water</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WHEELS">Wheels</a> (D. p. 270), which has escaped the notice of his able biographer M. Lacroix. He observes, in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, that the simple <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of a resistance varying as the square of the velocity, which is so near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> cases, where a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of particles, proportional to the velocity, strikes, in a given <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, upon a small exposed surface with a force also proportional to the velocity, is totally inapplicable to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of a confined stream upon the floatsboards of a wheel, since in this instance, the number of particles concerned cannot vary materially with the velocity, the whole stream being supposed to operate in all cases upon the successive floatsboards; so that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> would require us to suppose the force in this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> nearly proportional to the simple relative velocity; a conclusion which agrees remarkably well with the experiments of some practical authors. The same volume contains a continuation of M. Borda's researches relating to the resistance of oblique surfaces (E. Mem. Ac. Par. 1767, p. 495), with a statement of experiments still more conclusively confuting the received hypothesis respecting oblique impulse than his former investigations had done. We also find in it an Essay on isoperimetrical problems (F. p. 551), in which it is shown that Euler's method of treating them, which had been in great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> abandoned by its equally profound and candid author, in favour of the more general and more elegant calculations of Lagrange, was still capable of affording all the results that had been derived from the method of variations; and he even pointed out some deficiencies in the first memoir of Lagrange, which contained the detail of his ingenious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. These investigations of M. Borda afford collateral <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the strict truth of the demonstrations of both his great predecessors; and though they have been little employed by later mathematicians, yet it must be admitted to be of some importance, in enabling us to appreciate the value of a new <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of calculation, to determine whether its results are or are not such as might be obtained with almost equal convenience by methods before in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. His memoir, inserted in the collection of the Academy for 1768 (G. Mem. Ac. Par. 1768, p. 18), is devoted exclusively to the theory of pumps; and he considers especially the effect of the passage of the fluid through valves and other contracted parts in diminishing the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the discharge. His results are derived from the principle of the preservation of the living force or energy of a system of bodies, throughout all the vicissitudes of its motions, which had before been employed with success by Daniel Bernoulli in problems of a similar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; but it was not until the experiments of Biot had afforded sufficient grounds for the determination of the friction of fluids, that cases of this kind could be submitted to exact calculation. In his Essay on the curve described by cannon-balls, published among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> for 1769 (H. Mem. Ac. Par. 1769, p. 247), he has greatly simplified the practical theory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROJECTILES">projectiles</a>, which had been treated in a satisfactory though very general manner by John Bernoulli, and had been reduced into a much more convenient form by Euler. M. Borda has substituted some approximate expressions for the true value of the density of the air, and has thus been enabled to integrate equations which, in their more strictly correct form, had resisted the powers of Euler himself; and he has justified the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> of the formulas thus obtained by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with experiment. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time his talents were very actively employed in the naval <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which he entered in 1767, by the nomination of M. Praslin. The time-keepers of Le Roy and Berthoud were beginning to rival those of the English artists, and the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> ordered several vessels to be fitted out for cruises, in order to examine the accuracy of these time-keepers. M. Borda was appointed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> on board of the Flore, and acted jointly with M. Pingré as a delegate of the Academy of Sciences for the purposes of the expedition. The voyage occupied about a year, and extended to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a>, the West Indies, Newfoundland, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. M. Borda had a considerable share in the account which was published of the observations; and the formula which he has here given for the correction of the effects of refraction and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLAX">parallax</a> is considered as equally elegant and convenient. He also presented to the academy a separate memoir on the results of the expedition. (I. Voyage pour éprouver les Montres de Le Roy. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. K. Mem. Ac. Par. 1773, p. 258.) After an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of six weeks, these watches were found capable of determining the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> within about fifteen minutes of the truth. In order to supply some deficiencies in the observations made at the Canaries, Borda was sent out a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time, with the Boussole and the Esquiple; and he published, after his return (L.), a very correct and highly finished map of these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. He was soon afterwards promoted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, and served under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> d'Estaing as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-general, an appointment nearly similar to that of our captains of the fleet. In this capacity he observed the inconvenience of too great a variety in the sizes of the vessels constituting a fleet, and proposed to abolish the class of fifty and of sixty-four <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> ships, as too small for the line of battle, and to build ships of three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RATES">rates</a> only, the lowest carrying seventy-four guns, so that a smaller quantity of stores should require to be kept ready for use in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCK">dock</a>-yards, than when ships of more various dimensions were to be refitted. In 1780 he had the command of the Guerrier, and in 1781 of the Solitaire, which was taken after a gallant resistance by an English squadron. He was thus compelled to pay a visit to Great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, but was immediately set at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> upon his parole. He proposed to the academy in this year (M. Mem. Ac. Par. 1781), a mode of regulating elections, which was adopted by that body. Its peculiarity consisted in having the names of the candidates arranged by each voter in a certain order, and collecting the numbers expressing the degrees of preference into separate results, so that the simple majority of voters did not necessarily establish the claim of any individual, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he was placed very low in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a> by any considerable number of those who voted against him. But it must be allowed that this mode of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> is by no means wholly unobjectionable. M. Borda appears to have rendered an essential service to the cultivators of practical <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> by the introduction and improvement of the repeating circle, although this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> has probably been less employed in Great Britain than elsewhere, on account of the greater perfection of those which were previously in common use. It had been suggested by Mayer in 1767, that a circle with two movable sights would enable us to observe a given angle a great number of times in succession, and to add together the results, without any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-READING">reading</a> them off, and thus to obtain a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of precision equal to that of much larger and better instruments of a different construction; but the proposal had been little noticed until ten years afterwards, when Borda pursued the path pointed out by Mayer, and trained Lenoir, then a young and unlicensed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, to the execution of the improved instrument, notwithstanding the opposition of the rival opticians, and the want of encouragement from the opulent public. He published in 1787 (N.) his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> and Use of the Reflecting Circle, with different Methods for Calculating the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">Principal</a> Observations of Nautical Astronomy; but the officers of the French <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, for whom this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was intended, appear to have profited but little by his instructions. His instrument was, however, much employed in the operations for determining the length of the terrestrial meridian; and he himself took <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the experiments required for ascertaining the length of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a>, and for the comparison of the different standards with each other. He invented some very ingenious methods of overcoming the difficulties which present themselves in the pursuit of these objects; but he was interrupted in his researches by the horrors of the Revolution, nor did he live to see the whole of the operations completed. He endeavoured, also, to promote the introduction of the new mode of subdividing the circle, by the laborious computation of Tables of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOGARITHMS">Logarithms</a> (O. 4to, Par. 1801) adapted to decimal parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>; a work in which he was assisted by M. Delambre. From the increasing indisposition of M. Callet, who had undertaken to correct the proofs of these tables, some very material errors had been committed in the first half of the tables, and M. Borda thought it necessary to cancel a great number of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>; and in order to meet the expense thus entailed on him, he was obliged to dispose of an estate which he had lately acquired in his native place. He was also engaged, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his life, in the measurement of the force of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">magnetism</a>, and in the calculations of astronomical refraction. His <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> had been threatened for several successive winters, and he died the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1799. In his manners he was animated and unaffected. He avoided those who sought his acquaintance merely from the vanity of being intimate with a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> of talents, whatever pretensions to importance they might derive from their casual relations to general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. He never married; and he was too much absorbed in the pursuit of science to associate with a very extensive circle even of private friends. Though not a man of learning, he was not deficient in literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; and he was, in particular, a passionate admirer of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. He seems to have possessed a considerable share of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> tact and sagacity which was so remarkable in Newton, and which we also discover in the works of Daniel Bernoulli; enabling them, like a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>, to elude the insurmountable difficulties with which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> investigations are often encumbered; while Euler, on the contrary, as M. Lacroix most truly observes, seems to have taken <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in searching for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which would give scope to his analytical ingenuity, although wholly foreign to the physical investigations which had first led him to the difficulties in question. It would have been fortunate for the progress of science if some of the most celebrated of M. Borda's countrymen had profited by his example, in studying to attain that unostentatious simplicity which is the last result of the highest cultivation. (Lacroix, in Rapport des Travaux de la Société Philomathique, vol. iv. 8. Par. 1800.)

BORDE

Pages 48-48

ANDREW, a physician, jocularly styled by himself Andreas Perforatus, was born at Pevensey in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, about A.D. 1500, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. After travelling through various parts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, he settled first at Pevensey, afterwards at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, and finally in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he is said to have become a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Physicians, and to have acted in the capacity of physician to Henry VIII. But notwithstanding his success in his profession, he died insolvent in the Fleet prison in 1549. He was the author of several small jocular histories and cheap books, such as formed the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-READING">reading</a> of those times. He descended to the arts of a mountebank, making humorous speeches at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> to attract the people; and from him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> "Merry Andrew" is said to be derived. Wood says that "he was esteemed a noted poet, a witty and ingenious person, and an excellent physician."

BORDEAUX

Pages 48-48

an important commercial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and seaport town of France, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of an arrondissement of the same name, and also of the department of Gironde.
