href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">Battle</a> of Dettingen.—Intended invasion of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> by France.—Battle of Fontenoy.—Capture of Louisburg.—Landing of the Pretender in Scotland.—Battle of Gladsmuir.—Advance into England.—Conquest in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>.—Retreat to the Highlands.—Army from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>.—Siege of Stirling Castle.—Battle of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALKIRK">Falkirk</a>.—Advance of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, and retreat of the Rebels.—Battle of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CULLODEN">Culloden</a>.—Cruelty of Cumberland.—Subsequent adventures and escape of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Edward.—Execution of Rebels.—Policy of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a> in regard to the Highlands of Scotland.—Allies defeated in Flanders.—Losses sustained by the French in other parts.—Peace of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle.—<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">Death</a> of the Prince of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>.—Hostilities renewed.—<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a> invaded.—Execution of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Byng.—<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">Treaty</a> with Russia.—Opposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>.—New Commissions of the European powers.—Unsuccessful expedition against France.—<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACCUSATION">Accusation</a> of Mr Pitt to office.—Success of the British arms in both hemispheres.—Quebec taken and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> reduced.—Misconduct of Cumberland in Germany.—<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPITULATION">Capitulation</a> of Closter <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a>.—French defeated at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINDEN">Minden</a>.—German war <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with various success.—Death of George II. On the accession of George II, who succeeded to his father in the forty-fourth year of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> parties into which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a> had so <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> been divided again changed their names, and were now called the Court and Country Parties. Throughout the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this reign there seem to have been two objects of controversy, which rose up in debate every session, and tried the strength of the opponents; namely, the national debt, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of forces to be kept in pay. The government, on the present king's accession, owed more than thirty millions of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; and although there was a long continuance of profound peace, yet this sum went on constantly increasing. How this could happen was much wondered at by the country party, and it was as constantly the business of the court to give plausible reasons for the increase. Hence demands for new supplies were made every session of parliament, for the purpose of securing friends upon the Continent, of guarding the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> from internal conspiracies, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> of enabling the ministry to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> vigorously in conjunction with the powers in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> abroad. It was vainly alleged that these expenses were incurred without foresight or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>; and that the increase of the national debt, by multiplying and increasing taxes, would at last become an intolerable burden to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. These arguments were offered, canvassed, rejected; the court party was constantly victorious, and every demand was granted with equal cheerfulness and profusion. The next thing worthy of notice in the reign of George II is the Charitable Corporation. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of men had united themselves into a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> under this name, with the professed intention of lending money at legal <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to the poor upon small pledges, and to persons of higher <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> upon proper security. Their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> was at first limited to thirty thousand pounds; but they afterwards increased it to six hundred thousand. This money was supplied by subscription, and the care of conducting the capital was intrusted to a proper number of directors. The company having continued in existence for more than twenty years, the cashier, George Robinson, member for Marlow, and the warehouse-keeper, John Thomson, disappeared in one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and five hundred thousand pounds of capital were found to be sunk or embezzled by means which the proprietors could not discover. In a petition to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, therefore, they represented the manner in which they had been defrauded, and the distress to which many of them had in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> been reduced; and a secret committee having been appointed to examine into this grievance, a most iniquitous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of fraud was discovered, which had been carried on by Thompson and Robinson, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with some of the directors, for embezzling the capital and cheating the proprietors. Many persons of rank and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> were concerned in this infamous confederacy; and even some of the first <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in the nation did not escape censure. No less than six members of parliament were expelled for the most sordid acts of knavery; Sir Robert Sutton, Sir Archibald <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRANT">Grant</a>, and George Robinson, for their frauds in the management of the Charitable Corporation scheme; Dennis Bond and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">Sergeant</a> Burch, for a fraudulent <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Derwentwater's estate; and John <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARD">Ward</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HACKNEY">Hackney</a>, for the crime of forgery. It was at this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> asserted in the House of Lords that not one <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> of the forfeited estates had ever been applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the public, but had become the reward of fraud, villainy, and profligacy. This happened in the year 1731. In 1732 a scheme was formed by Sir Robert Walpole of fixing a general excise; and he introduced it by enumerating the frauds practised by the factors in London employed in selling the American <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>. To prevent these frauds, he proposed, that instead of having the customs levied in the usual manner, all the tobacco to be hereafter imported should be lodged in warehouses appointed for that purpose by the officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and should from thence be sold, upon paying the duty of fourpence a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, whenever the proprietor found a purchaser. This proposal raised a violent ferment, both within and without doors; and at last the fury of the people was worked up to such a pitch, that the parliament-house was surrounded by multitudes, who intimidated the ministry, and compelled them to abandon the scheme. The miscarriage of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BILL">bill</a> was celebrated with public rejoicings in London and Westminster, and the minister was burned in effigy by the populace of London. On this occasion an attempt was made to repeal the septennial bill, and bring back <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRIENNIAL">triennial</a> parliaments, as settled at the Revolution. But notwithstanding the warmth of the opposition, the ministry, exerting all their strength, proved victorious, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> was defeated. However, as on this occasion the country party seemed to have gained strength, it was thought proper to dissolve the parliament, and to summon another by the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>. But the same disputes were carried on in this as in the former parliament. New subjects of controversy offered every day, and both sides were eager to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> them. A convention agreed on by the ministry with Spain became an object of warm altercation. By this the court of Spain had agreed to pay ninety-five thousand pounds to the English, as a satisfaction for all demands, and to discharge the whole in four months from the day of ratification; but this stipulation was considered as not containing an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> for the damages which had been sustained, and which were said to amount to three hundred and forty thousand pounds. A violent discussion ensued, in the course of which the minister was provoked into unusual vehemence, and branded the opposite party with the appellation of traitors. But he was, as usual, victorious; and the country party finding themselves out-numbered and out-voted in every debate, resolved to withdraw for ever; while Walpole, thus left without opposition, took the opportunity of passing several useful laws in their absence, in order to render his opponents odious or contemptible to the country. In 1739 a new war commenced with Spain. Ever since the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, the Spaniards in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> had insulted and distressed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Great Britain; whilst the British <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, on the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, had endeavoured to carry on an illicit trade with their dominions. As a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> logwood in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPEACHY">Campeachy</a>, claimed by the British, gave them frequent opportunities of introducing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRABAND">contraband</a> commodities into the continent, the Spaniards resolved to put a stop to the evil by refusing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to cut logwood in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The guardacostas exercised great severities, and many British subjects were sent to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of Potosi. One remonstrance followed another to the court of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>; but the only answers given were promises of inquiry, which produced no reformation. Accordingly, in 1739 war was declared with all proper solemnity; and soon after Admiral <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VERNON">Vernon</a>, with only six ships, destroyed all the fortifications of Puerto Bello, and came away victorious, with scarcely the loss of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>. As the war was thus successfully begun, supplies were cheerfully granted to prosecute it with all imaginable vigour. Commodore Anson was sent with a squadron of ships to distress the enemy in the South Seas, and to co-operate occasionally with Admiral Vernon across the Isthmus of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a>. This squadron was designed to act a part subordinate to a formidable armament which was to be sent against <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> or New Spain; but through the mismanagement of the ministry both these schemes were frustrated. Anson was detained till too late in the season, when he set out with five ships of the line, a frigate, two store-ships, and about fourteen hundred men. But having entered the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> at the most unfavourable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the year, he encountered terrible storms; his fleet was dispersed, and his crew deplorably afflicted with scurvy, so that with the utmost difficulty he reached the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Juan Fernandez. Here, however, he was joined by one ship and a frigate of seventeen guns, and sailing from thence along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, he plundered and burnt the town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAITA">Paita</a>. He next traversed the Pacific, in hopes of meeting with one of the rich galleons which traded from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PHILIPPINE_ISLANDS">Philippine <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a> to Mexico. Having refreshed his men at the island of Tinian, he set sail for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; and returning by the same route, he at last discovered the galleon, which he engaged and took; and with this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, valued at upwards of three hundred thousand pounds, together with other captures to the value of about as much more, he returned home, after a voyage of three years. By this expedition the public sustained the loss of a fine squadron of ships, but a few individuals became possessed of immense fortunes. Another expedition which was fitted out ended still more unfortunately. The armament consisted of twenty-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> sail of the line, and an almost equal number of frigates, furnished with all kinds of warlike stores, near fifteen thousand seamen, and as many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> forces. The most sanguine hopes of success were entertained; but the ministry detained the fleet without any visible reason till the season for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> in America was nearly past. At last, however, the squadron arrived before Cartagena, and soon captured the strong forts which defended the harbour. But though by this means they were enabled to approach nearer the town, they still found great difficulties before them. From an erroneous <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that the ships could not get near enough to batter the town, and that therefore the remaining forts must be attempted by escalade, this dangerous experiment was tried; but the guides were slain by the enemy's fire, and the forces, mistaking their way, instead of attempting the weakest part of the fort, attacked the strongest, where they were exposed to the fire of the whole town. Their scaling ladders were also too short; and at last, after sustaining a dreadful fire with great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> for some hours, they retreated, leaving six hundred men dead on the spot. The ravages of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> now began to prove more dreadful than the casualties of war; and the rainy season commenced with such violence, that it was found impossible for the troops to continue in their encampment. And, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> to aggravate these calamities, dissension arose between the commanders of the sea and land forces, who blamed each other, and at last could only be brought to agree in one mortifying <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, namely, the re-embarkation of the troops. The miscarriage of this enterprise produced the greatest discontentments, more especially as other causes of complaint occurred at the same time. Sir John Norris had twice sailed to the coast of Spain at the head of a powerful squadron, without effecting anything of consequence. The commerce of Britain was greatly annoyed by the Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a>, who had taken upwards of four hundred ships since the commencement of the war; whilst the British fleets remained quite inactive, and suffered one loss after another, without endeavouring in the least to make proper <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-REPRISALS">reprisals</a>. These discontentants burst out all at once against Sir Robert Walpole; a majority was formed in the House of Commons in opposition to the ministry of which he was the head; he was created Earl of Orford; and the parliament having adjourned for a few days on purpose, he resigned all his employments. The removal of this minister gave universal satisfaction. His antagonists entertained great hopes of seeing him punished; but he had laid his schemes too well to be under any apprehensions on that account; and, in fact, the new ministry had no sooner got into office than they trod in the footsteps of those whom they had so much exclaimed against. The nation had now become disgusted with naval operations. The people desired a renewal of their victories in Flanders, and the king ardently joined in the same wish. An army of sixteen thousand men was therefore shipped and sent to Flanders, to take part in the quarrels that were then beginning to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out on the Continent. Immense triumphs were expected from this undertaking; but it was somehow forgotten that the army was not now commanded by John Duke of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>. In order to give some notion of the origin of these continental disputes, it is necessary to go back for several years. After the Duke of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, regent of France, died, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Fleury undertook to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the confusion in which the kingdom was then involved; and under him France repaired her losses, and enriched herself by means of commerce. During the long <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of peace which this minister's counsels had procured for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, two powers, hitherto disregarded, began to attract the notice and the jealousy of the neighbouring nations. These were Russia and Prussia, both of which had been gradually rising into power and consequence. The other states were but little prepared to renew the war. The empire remained under the government of Charles VI., who had been placed on the throne by the treaty of Utrecht; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> continued to languish, from the destructive projects of Charles XII.; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> was powerful enough, but inclined to peace; and part of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> still remained subject to those princes who had been imposed upon it in consequence of foreign treaties. All these states, however, continued to enjoy profound peace, until the death of Augustus king of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; an event by which a general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> was once more kindled in Europe. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, assisted by the arms of Russia, declared for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, the son of the deceased king; whilst France, on the other hand, espoused the cause of Stanislaus, who had long ago been nominated king of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a> by Charles of Sweden, and whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> the king of France had since married. Stanislaus was gladly received at Danzig, and acknowledged as king of Poland; but having been besieged there by ten thousand Russians, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was taken, and he himself with difficulty made his escape. France, however, still resolved to assist him, as the most effectual method of distressing the house of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>; and her views were seconded by Spain and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, both of which hoped to be enriched by the spoils of Austria. A French army, therefore, overran the empire, under the conduct of the old Marshal Villars; whilst the Duke of Montemar, the Spanish general, was equally victorious in the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. The emperor was soon obliged to sue for peace, which was granted; but Stanislaus was neglected in the treaty, it having been stipulated that he should renounce all claim to the kingdom of Poland; while the emperor gratified France with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Lorraine, and other valuable territories, as an indemnification. The emperor dying in the year 1740, the French thought the opportunity favourable for their ambition, and, regardless of treaties, particularly that called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAGMATIC_SANCTION">Pragmatic Sanction</a>, by which the late emperor's dominions were settled upon his daughter, caused the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTOR">Elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> to be crowned emperor. Thus the queen of Hungary, daughter of Charles VI., was at once stripped of her inheritance, and left for a whole year without any hopes of succour; and at the same time she lost the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a> by an irruption of the young king of Prussia, who took the opportunity of her defenceless condition to renew his pretensions to that province. France, Saxony, and Bavaria, attacked the rest of her dominions; and Britain was the only ally who seemed willing to assist her; but Sardinia, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and Russia, soon afterwards concurred in the same views. It must be owned that the only reason which Britain had for interfering in these disputes was, that the security of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> depended upon nicely balancing the different interests of the empire; but the ministry were nevertheless willing to gratify the king by engaging the country in a war. His majesty informed the parliament that he had sent a body of British forces into the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, which he had augmented by sixteen thousand Hanoverians, to operate a diversion on the side of France, in favour of the queen of Hungary. But when the supplies by which this additional number of Hanoverian troops was to receive pay from Britain for defending their own cause came to be considered, violent parliamentary debates ensued; and although the ministry carried their point by the strength of numbers, they had but little reason to boast of their victory. Yet, however prejudicial these continental <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> might be to the true interests of Great Britain, they effectually retrieved the queen of Hungary's affairs, and soon turned the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of victory in her favour. The French were driven out of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>; while her general, Prince Charles of Lorraine, at the head of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> army, invaded the dominions of Bavaria. Her rival, the nominal emperor, was obliged to fly before her; and, abandoned by his allies, as well as stripped of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> domains, he retired to Frankfort, where he lived in obscurity. Meanwhile the British and Hanoverian army advanced in order to effect a junction with that under Prince Charles, by which they would have outnumbered their enemies; and to prevent this the French opposed an army of sixty thousand men, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, under the command of Marshal de Noailles, who posted his troops on the eastern side of that river. The British army was commanded by the Earl of Stair, who, although he had learned the art of war under Eugene and Marlborough, suffered himself to be inclosed by the enemy on every side, near a village called Dettingen; and in this situation the whole army, with the king himself, who had by this time arrived in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, must have been taken prisoners, had the French behaved with ordinary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>. But their impetuosity saved the combined force from destruction. They passed a defile which they ought to have contented themselves with guarding, and, under the conduct of the Duke de Grammont, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> the British foot with great fury; but they were received with unshaken firmness, and at last obliged to repass the Maine with precipitation, and the loss of about five thousand men. The British monarch, who was present in the battle, displayed equal courage and conduct, and in some measure atoned for an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> which might otherwise have proved fatal. But though the British were victorious in this engagement, the French were very little disconcerted by it. They opposed Prince Charles, and interrupted his attempts to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; and in Italy they also gained some advantages; but their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> hopes were placed on an intended invasion of England. From the violence of parliamentary disputes in England, France had been persuaded that the country was ripe for a revolution, and only wanted the presence of the pretender to bring about a change. An invasion was therefore projected; the troops destined for the expedition amounted to fifteen thousand; and preparations were made for embarking them at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a> and some of the ports nearest to England, under the eye of the young pretender. The Duke de Roquefeuille, with twenty ships of the line, was to see them safely landed on the opposite shore; and the famous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Saxe was to command them when disembarked. But the whole project was disconcerted by the appearance of Sir John Norris, with a superior fleet, which obliged the French squadron to put back; while a severe <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> damaged their transports, and thus entirely frustrated the scheme of a sudden <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>. But the national joy for Sir John Norris's success was soon damped by the miscarriage of Admirals Mathews and Lestock, who, through a misunderstanding, suffered a French fleet of thirty-four sail to escape them near <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOULON">Toulon</a>. In the Netherlands the British arms were also attended with ill success. The French had there assembled an army of a hundred and twenty thousand men, commanded by Count Saxe, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of the late king of Poland, and an officer of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. The English were under Reign of the Duke of Cumberland, whose army was much inferior in number to that of the enemy, whilst in point of knowledge of war the disparity between him and the French general was still greater. Count Saxe, therefore, carried all before him. In the year 1743 he besieged Fribourg, and in the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of 1744 he invested the strong city of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOURNAY">Tournay</a>. To <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the place, if possible, the allies resolved to hazard an engagement; and this brought on the memorable battle of Fontenoy. The French were posted behind the town of that name, on some eminences which completely commanded the defile which formed the only approach to the position. At two in the morning the assailants quitted their camp, and about nine the British infantry, formed in a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, attacked the centre of the enemy's line, which was drawn up in a sort of avenue to receive them. But from the confined <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the ground, the obstinacy of the resistance in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and the flanking fire kept up from some woody heights which dominated over the defile, this fine body of troops was never able to develop its attack nor to clear the defile; yet, in spite of every effort of the enemy, it maintained its ground till three in the afternoon, preserving its formation unbroken, notwithstanding the plunging fire of the French <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, and the concentrated musketry of their infantry, to which it was without intermission exposed; and at last it retired in perfect order, facing round at intervals, and checking the pursuit of the enemy. The loss of the allies amounted to twelve thousand men, and that of the French was even greater; but the victory nevertheless gave them the superiority during the rest of the campaign, as well as during the remainder of the war. The capture of Tournay was the first fruit of this dear-bought success; and though the Elector of Bavaria, whom they had proclaimed emperor, was now dead, the French were too much elated by success to relax in their operations against the allies. To <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> the defeat at Fontenoy, however, Admirals Rowley and Warren retrieved the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the British <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>, and made several rich captures at sea. The fortress of Louisbourg, a place of great consequence to the British commerce, surrendered to General Pepperell; and a short time afterwards two French East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> ships, and a Spanish ship from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> laden with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, put into the harbour, supposing it still their own, and were taken. During this gleam of returning success, Charles Edward, the son of the old pretender to the British crown, resolved to make an attempt to recover what he called his right. Being furnished with some money from France, he embarked for Scotland on board of a small frigate, accompanied by the Marquis of Tullibardine, Sir Thomas Sheridan, and some others; and for the conquest of the whole British empire, he only brought with him seven officers, and arms for two thousand men. Fortune, however, seemed nowise more favourable to this attempt than to others similar to it. His convoy, a ship of sixty guns, was so disabled in an engagement with an English man of war, that it was obliged to return to Brest, whilst he continued his course to the western parts of Scotland. On the 27th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1745 he landed on the coast of Lochaber, and was in a little time joined by the Highlanders to the number of fifteen hundred men. The ministry at first could scarcely be induced to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> the story of his arrival; but when it could no longer be doubted, they sent Sir John Cope with a small body of forces to oppose his progress. A favourable opportunity offered for striking a blow at Corryarick; but Cope, who seems to have been equally devoid of conduct and of energy, withdrew to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, thus uncovering the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to the low country. The young adventurer, availing himself of this blunder, immediately marched to the south, and arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>, where he performed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of proclaiming his father king of Great Britain. He then proceeded towards <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and, his forces continually increasing, entered the capital without opposition; but he was unable, from want of cannon, to reduce the castle. Here he again proclaimed his father; and promised to dissolve the union, which was still considered as one of the national grievances. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time Sir John Cope, having arrived from Inverness, and been reinforced by two regiments of dragoons, resolved to give battle to the enemy. The insurgents, however, attacked him at Gladsmuir, near Prestonpans, and in a few minutes put him and his troops to flight, with the loss of five hundred men. This victory gave the insurgents great hopes, from the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> it produced; and had the pretender marched directly to England, the result might perhaps have been fatal to the House of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>. But he was amused by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of succours which in fact never arrived, and thus induced to remain in Edinburgh till the season for action was lost. He was joined, however, by the Earl of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KILMARNOCK">Kilmarnock</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BALMERINO">Balmerino</a>, Lords Cromarty, Elcho, Ogilvy, Pitshigo, and the eldest son of Lord Lovat, who with their vassals considerably increased his army; and Lord Lovat himself, so remarkable for his treachery, was favourably disposed towards the pretender, although unwilling to act openly for fear of the government. But whilst Charles was thus trifling away his time at Edinburgh, the British ministry were taking most effectual methods to oppose him. Six thousand Dutch troops, which had come over to assist the government, were dispatched northward under the command of General Wade; but this force was then in some measure incapable of acting, being prisoners of France upon parole, and under engagements not to oppose that power for a year. Be this as it may, however, the Duke of Cumberland arrived soon afterwards from Flanders, and was followed by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of dragoons and infantry, well disciplined and inured to action; whilst volunteers offered their services in every part of the kingdom. At last Charles resolved upon an irruption into England. He entered that country by the western border, and took the town of Carlisle; after which he continued his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">march</a> southwards, having received assurances that a considerable body of forces would be landed on the southern coasts to create a diversion in his favour. He established his head-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, where he was joined by between two and three hundred English formed into a regiment under the command of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Townley; and thence he pursued his march to Derby, intending to go by the way of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a> into Wales, where he hoped to be joined by a great number of malcontents; but in this he was prevented by the factions among his followers. Having now advanced within a hundred miles of London, that capital was thrown into the utmost consternation; and had he proceeded with the same expedition which he had hitherto used, he might perhaps have made himself <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it. But he was prevented from pursuing this or any other rational <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> by the discontented which began to prevail in his army. The young pretender was in fact but the nominal leader of his forces; and his generals, the Highland chiefs, were equally averse to subordination and ignorant of command. They now, however, became unanimous in their resolution to return to their own country; and Charles was forced to comply. Accordingly they retreated to Carlisle without sustaining any loss; and thence crossing the Eden and Solway, entered Scotland. They next marched to Glasgow, which was laid under severe contributions; and thence proceeding to Stirling, they were joined by Lord <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Gordon at the head of some forces which had been assembled in his absence. Other clans likewise came in; while some supplies of money re- Reign of George II. Regiments received from Spain, and some skirmishes with the royalists, in which he was victorious, caused the pretender's affairs to assume a much more promising aspect. Being joined by Lord Drummond, he invested the castle of Stirling, in the siege of which much valuable time was consumed to no purpose. General Hawley, who commanded a considerable body of forces near Edinburgh, undertook to raise the siege, and with this view advanced as far as Falkirk in order to give battle to the Highland army. After some time spent in mutual observation, an engagement ensued on the 17th <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1746, in which the king's troops were entirely defeated. The Highlanders advanced to the attack with their usual impetuosity, threw in a volley or two, and then <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> their claymores, rushed forward, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in hand, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> with the enemy. The onset proved irresistible; infantry and cavalry were intermingled in one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rout; and the whole artillery and tents of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> army fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the conquerors. But the victory of Falkirk was the last of the triumphs of the rebel army. The Duke of Cumberland having arrived, put himself at the head of the troops at Edinburgh, amounting to about fourteen thousand men; and with these he marched to Aberdeen, where he was joined by several of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> attached to the house of Hanover, the enemy in the mean time retreating before him. He next advanced to the banks of the Spey, a deep and rapid river, where the Highlanders might have successfully disputed his passage; but their mutual contentions had now risen to such a height that they could scarce agree in anything. At last, however, they resolved to make a stand, and for this purpose selected Drummosie Muir, near Culoden, nine miles distant from Inverness; the only ground in the whole country where cavalry and artillery, the two arms which they had most reason to dread, could act with effect against them. Their numbers amounted to about eight thousand; and after an abortive attempt to surprise the royal army at Nairn, they returned to their position and drew out to receive the attack. At one in the afternoon of the 15th of April 1746, the cannonading commenced; and whilst the artillery of the rebels, from being miserably served, did little or no execution, that of the royal army, at every discharge, made frightful gaps in the Highland ranks. During the continuance of the cannonade, Cumberland observing that the right of the Highlanders was covered by a wall, ordered a body of men to advance and pull it <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. The Campbells, to whom this service was committed, promptly obeyed the order; and the right wing of the Highlanders being thus uncovered, they became exposed to a flanking fire as well as to that in front, which was now kept up with the greatest vivacity. In this trying situation a body, chiefly Atholemen, about nineteen hundred strong, unable any longer to sustain the galling fire which was poured on their ranks, and conscious that their real strength lay in close <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, advanced to the attack sword in hand; broke through Burrell's and Monro's regiments in an instant; and pressed on, with diminished numbers but dauntless resolution, against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> line of the royal army, amidst a concentrated and terrible fire from every <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> that could be brought to bear upon them. The second line steadily awaited the onset of this forlorn hope, reserving their fire till it came quite close, when a destructive volley was thrown in, while Wolfe's regiment, formed en potence, opened at the same instant a flanking fire. The force of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> was thus completely broken; a few and but a few of the assailants escaped; and the bravest, who did not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> by the murderous fire, perished in a desperate conflict with the English bayonets. Lochiel, advancing at the head of a small band, who had survived the encounter with the first line, was wounded in both ankles by a grape-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> while in the act of charging the second line; and in this state he was carried off the field by his two brothers, between whom <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> had advanced. Macdonald of Keppoch was also rushing on in like manner to the attack, when, receiving a wound which brought him to the ground, he was conjured by a friend not to throw away his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, but to retire and rejoin the main body; but desiring his friend to provide for his own safety, Macdonald got upon his legs, and, whilst preparing again to advance, received another shot, by which he fell to rise no more. Most of the chiefs who commanded the body that advanced to the charge, and almost every man in the front ranks, were killed. Unfortunately the Highland regiments on the left did not advance to close combat, or support the gallant attack which has <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> been described; had they done so, the issue might have been very different. After exchanging a volley or two with the right wing of the duke's army, and answering the fire of some dragoons who hovered near, they retreated, and separating into small parties, were cut up in detail, losing more men in proportion than the brave band who had made so gallant and vigorous an effort to retrieve the fortune of the day. In less than thirty minutes the battle was lost, and with it a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> period was put to all the hopes of the young adventurer. The conquerors behaved with the greatest cruelty, refusing <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> to the wounded, the unarmed, and the defenseless; and some were slain who had only been spectators of the combat; whilst <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were seen to anticipate the base employment of the executioner. The duke, immediately after the action, ordered thirty-six deserters to be executed; the conquerors spread terror wherever they went; and in a short time the whole country around became one dreadful scene of plunder, slaughter, and desolation. Immediately after the battle, the pretender fled with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of Fitzjames's cavalry; and when their horses were fatigued, they both alighted, and separately sought for safety. There is a striking resemblance between the adventures of Charles II. after the battle of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, and those of the pretender after the battle of Culloden. For several days he wandered through the country; sometimes he found refuge in caves and cottages, without any attendants at all; sometimes he lay in forests with one or two companions of his distress, continually pursued by the troops, there being a reward of L30,000 offered for taking him either dead or alive. In the course of his adventures he had occasion to trust his life to the fidelity of above fifty individuals, not one of whom could be prevailed on, even by so great a reward as that which was offered, to betray him whom they looked upon as the son of their king. For six months the unfortunate Charles continued to wander in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Glengarry, often hemmed round by his pursuers, but still rescued, by some providential accident, from the impending danger. At length a privateer of St Malo, hired by his adherents, having arrived in Lochranza, he embarked on board that vessel for France. At this time he was reduced to a state of inexpressible wretchedness, being clad in a short coat of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> frize, threadbare, over which was a common Highland plaid girt round him by a belt, from which hung a pistol and dagger. He had not been shifted for many weeks; his eyes were hollow, his visage was wan, and his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> greatly impaired by famine and fatigue. Accompanied by Sullivan and Sheridan, two Irish adherents, who had shared all his calamities, together with Cameron of Lochiel, his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, and a few other exiles, he set sail for France, and, after having been chased by two English men of war, arrived in safety at a place called Roscoff, near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORLAIX">Morlaix</a>, in Bretagne. While the pretender was thus pursued, the scaffolds and gibbets were preparing for his brave adherents. Seventeen officers were hanged, drawn, and quartered, at Kenning- Reign of ton Common, in the neighbourhood of London: nine were executed in the same manner at Carlisle, and eleven at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a>. A few obtained pardons, and a considerable number of the common men were transported to America. The Earls of Kilmarnock and Cromarty, and Lord Balmerino, were tried and found guilty of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. Cromarty was pardoned, but Kilmarnock and Balmerino were executed; as was also Mr Radcliffe, brother to the Earl of Derwentwater, who received <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon a former conviction. Lord Lovat was tried, and suffered some time afterwards. Immediately after the suppression of the rebellion, the legislature undertook to establish regulations in Scotland, conducive to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of the people and the tranquillity of the united kingdoms. The Highlanders had till that time continued to wear the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> dress of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and never went without arms; in consequence of which they considered themselves as a body of people distinct from the rest of the nation, and were ready upon the shortest notice to second the projects of their chiefs. Their habits were now reformed by an act of legislature, and they were compelled to wear clothes of the common fashion. But what contributed still more to destroy the spirit of clanship was the abolition of the hereditary jurisdictions which their chieftains exercised over them. The power of the chiefs was totally destroyed, and every subject in that part of the kingdom was liberated from the state of vassalage in which they had formerly lived. Soon after the battle of Culloden the Duke of Cumberland proceeded to Flanders, where he resumed the command of the army, to which he was by no means equal. The French carried every thing before them, and reduced under their dominion all the strong places which had been taken by the Duke of Marlborough, and formed a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to the united provinces. They gained a considerable victory near Rocoux, though at a great sacrifice of men, which, however, they could easily spare, as they were much more numerous than their adversaries; and another victory which they obtained at Lafeldt served to depress still further the spirit of the allied army. But the taking of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol4.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-Zoom, the strongest fortification of Brabant, was the event which naturally reduced the Dutch to the greatest alarm and distress. These victories and successes in Flanders, however, were counterbalanced by almost equal disappointments. In Italy, the brother of Marshal Belleisle, attempting to penetrate into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a> at the head of thirty-four thousand men, was defeated and killed. A fleet had been fitted out for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Breton, but without success; and two others were equipped, the one to make a descent upon the British colonies in America, and the other to carry on the operations in the East Indies; but these were attacked by Anson and Warren, and nine of their ships taken. Soon after this, Commodore Fox, with six ships of war, took above forty French ships richly laden from St Domingo; and about the same time the French fleet was defeated by Admiral Hawke, who took seven ships of the line and several frigates. For a long time <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> had been desirous of peace, and this desire he even expressed to Sir John Ligonier, who had been taken prisoner at the battle of Lafeldt. But now the bad success of his admirals at sea, and his armies in Italy, the frequent bankruptcies of his merchants at home, and the election of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a> in Holland, who gave spirit to the opposition—all these contributed to make him weary of the war, and to propose terms of accommodation. This was what the allies had long wished for, but had been ashamed to demand. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> was therefore held at Aix-la-Chapelle, and a treaty concluded, by which it was provided that all prisoners on each side should be mutually given up, and all conquests restored; that the duchies of Parma, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUASTALLA">Guastalla</a>, should be ceded to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, heir-apparent to the Spanish crown, and after his return to the house of Austria; that the fortifications of Dunkirk towards the sea should be demolished; that the British ship annually sent with slaves to the coast of New Spain should have this privilege continued for four years; that the king of Prussia should be confirmed in the possession of Silesia; and that the queen of Hungary should be secured in the possession of her patrimonial dominions. But the most mortifying clause was, that the king of Great Britain should, immediately after the ratification of this treaty, send two persons of rank to France as hostages, until restitution should be made of Cape Breton and all other British conquests during the war. No mention whatever was made of the searching of British vessels in the American seas, though this was the original cause of the quarrel; the limits of their respective possessions in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> America were not ascertained; nor did they receive any equivalent for those forts which they had restored to the enemy. In the year 1751 Frederick prince of Wales died of a pleurisy, which was not thought at first to be in any way dangerous. He was much regretted, for his good-nature had rendered him popular, and those who opposed the present administration had grounded their hopes of redress upon his accession to the throne. Some time before this, in the year 1749, a scheme had been entered upon, from which the nation in general anticipated great advantages; namely, encouraging those who had been discharged from the army or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> to become settlers in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a>, a country <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, barren, and almost incapable of cultivation. Nevertheless, on account of this barren spot, the English and French actually renewed the war. The possession of this country was reckoned necessary for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the English colonies to the north, and for preserving their superiority in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> in that part of the world. The French, however, who had been long settled in the back parts, resolved to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> every method to dispossess the new comers, and spirited up the Indians to begin hostilities. Another source of dispute also sprung up in the same part of the world. The French, pretending to have first discovered the mouth of the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>, claimed the whole adjacent country towards New Mexico on the east, and to the Appalachian Mountains on the west; and, in order to assert their claims, as they found several English who had settled beyond these mountains, they dispossessed them of their new settlements, and built such forts as were calculated to command the whole country round about. Negotiations and mutual accusations were followed by hostilities; and in 1756 four operations were undertaken by the British in America at once. Colonel Monckton had orders to drive the French from the province of Nova Scotia; General Johnson was sent against Crown Point; General Shirley against <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NIAGARA">Niagara</a>, to secure the forts on the river; and General Braddock against Fort du Quesne. In these expeditions Monckton was successful; Johnson was also victorious, though he failed in taking the fort against which he was sent; Shirley was thought to have lost the season of operation by delay; and Braddock was defeated and killed. But, in return for this failure of success, the British made reprisals at sea; and here they were so successful that the French navy was unable to recover itself during the continuance of the war. The first measure of the French was to threaten an invasion. Several bodies of their troops were sent down to the coasts opposite Britain, and these were instructed in the manner of embarking and relanding from flat-bottomed boats, which were made in great numbers for the purpose. The number of men amounted to fifty thousand, but all discovered the utmost reluctance to the undertaking. The ministry were greatly alarmed, and applied to the Dutch for six thousand men, which they were by treaty obliged to furnish in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> of invasion. But this supply was refused, the Dutch alleging that their treaty was to send the troops in case of an actual, and not of a threatened, invasion. The king, therefore, finding he could not reckon upon the Dutch forces till their assistance would be too late, desisted entirely from his demand; and the Dutch with great cordiality returned him thanks for withdrawing his request. Upon this ten thousand Hessians and Hanoverians were brought over; a proceeding which occasioned great discontent. The ministry were reviled for such disgraceful conduct, as if the nation was unable to defend itself; whereas the people only demanded a vigorous exertion of their own internal strength, and then feared no force that could be led to invade them. The threatened invasion, however, never took place. But a French army landed in Minorca, and invested the citadel of St Philips, which was reckoned the strongest in Europe, but the garrison was nevertheless weak, and not wise fitted to stand a vigorous siege. To raise this siege, Admiral Byng was dispatched with a squadron of ten men of war, with orders to relieve Minorca, or at any rate to throw a body of troops into the garrison. But this last he reckoned too hazardous an undertaking, nor did he even attempt it; and soon afterwards a French fleet appeared nearly equal in force to his own, when he resolved to act only on the defensive. The French advanced, and a slight engagement ensued with part of the English fleet; after which the enemy slowly withdrew, and no other opportunity occurred of coming to a close engagement. Upon this it was resolved in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of war to return to Gibraltar to refit, and agreed that the relief of Minorca was impracticable. For such pusillanimous, if not treacherous conduct, Byng was brought home under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a>, tried, condemned to death, and shot. He suffered with the greatest resolution, after delivering a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> filled with protestations of his innocence as to any treacherous intention. After the conquest of Minorca, the French declared that they would <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> all injuries which they might sustain in their colonies on the king of Britain's dominions in Germany. Upon this the court of London, eager to preserve Hanover, entered into a treaty with the court of Russia, by which it was stipulated that a body of fifty thousand Russians should be ready to act in the British service, in case Hanover should be invaded by the French; for which the Czarina was to receive L100,000 annually, to be paid in advance. But the treaty was opposed by the king of Prussia, who had long considered himself as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the interests of Germany, and was therefore alarmed at a treaty which threatened to deluge the empire with an army of barbarians. Besides, he was already apprised of an agreement between the Austrians and Russians, by which the latter were to enter the empire and strip him of his late conquest of Silesia. He therefore declared that he would not suffer any foreign forces to enter the empire, either as auxiliaries or principals; so that the king of Britain found himself obliged to drop his Russian connection, and conclude a treaty with the king of Prussia. As both monarchs wished only to prevent the invasion of Germany, they soon came to an agreement to assist each other mutually; and from this alliance a new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> took place among the European powers, quite opposite to the former one. Britain opposed France in America, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and on the ocean. France attacked Hanover, which the king of Prussia undertook to protect; whilst Britain promised him troops and money to assist his operations. Austria having aims on the dominions of Prussia, drew the Elector of Saxony into the same designs; and in these views the Austrians were seconded by France, Sweden, and Russia, who had hopes of acquiring a settlement in the west of Europe. Thus the king of Prussia launched into the tumult of war, having only the king of Britain for his ally; whilst the most powerful states of Europe were his antagonists. He now performed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of exploits which, taken as a whole, are not surpassed in the annals of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, and of which a particular account <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be given in the article PRUSSIA. The British ministry, in order to create a diversion in his favour, planned an enterprise against the coast of France; but the destination of the fleet equipped for this purpose was kept a profound secret. At last, however, it appeared before <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROCHEFORT">Rochefort</a>, where the commanders, having trifled away their time in deliberating how to proceed, took the little island of Aix, an easy and useless conquest, and soon afterwards returned home without attempting anything else. By this miscarriage the ministry were so discouraged that they had thoughts of abandoning the king of Prussia to his fate; and the king was actually meditating a negotiation of this nature, when he was prevented by the expostulations of his distressed ally. From motives of generosity, therefore, more than of interest, it was resolved to continue to assist him; and success, which had long fled from the British arms, once more began to return with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> splendour. It was in the East Indies where this return of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> first manifested itself; but the British conquests in the western part of the world speedily eclipsed those in the eastern. These successes must, in part at least, be ascribed to the vigorous administration of Mr William Pitt, who about this time came into power. An expedition was set on foot against Cape Breton, under General <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMHERST">Amherst</a> and Admiral Boscawen; another under General Abercrombie, against Crown Point and Ticonderago; and a third under Brigadier-General Forbes, against Fort du Quesne. The fortress of Louisbourg, which defended the island of Cape Breton, was strong both by nature and art; the garrison was numerous, the commander vigilant, and every precaution had been taken to prevent a landing; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of the British surmounted every obstacle; and the place having been surrendered by capitulation, its fortifications were demolished. The expedition against Fort du Quesne was equally successful; but that against Crown Point once more miscarried. General Abercrombie attacked the French in their intrenchments, but was repulsed with great slaughter, and obliged to retire to his camp at Lake George. But though in this respect the British arms were unsuccessful, yet, upon the whole, the campaign of 1758 ended greatly in their favour. The taking of Fort du Quesne served to remove from their colonies the terror of the incursions of the Indians, whilst it interrupted the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> along a chain of forts with which the French had environed the British settlements in America; and the succeeding campaign promised still greater success. In 1759 it was resolved to attack the French in several parts of their territory at once. General Amherst, with a body of twelve thousand men, was commanded to attack Crown Point; General Wolfe was to undertake the siege of Quebec; whilst General Prideaux and Sir William Johnson were to attempt a French fort near the cataracts of Niagara. This last expedition was the first that succeeded. The siege was begun with vigour, and promised an easy conquest; but General Prideaux being killed in the trenches by the bursting of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, the command devolved on General Johnson. A body of French troops, sensible of the importance of the place, attempted to relieve it, but were utterly defeated and dispersed; and soon afterwards the garrison surrendered prisoners of war. On his arrival at the forts of Crown Point and Ticonderago, Ge- Reign of neral Amberst found them deserted and destroyed. There George II now remained, therefore, but one decisive blow to be struck in order to reduce the whole of North America under the British dominion; namely, by the capture of Quebec, the capital of Canada. This expedition was commanded by Admiral Saunders and General Wolfe. The enterprise was attended with difficulties which appeared insurmountable; but all these were overcome by the admirable conduct of the general, and the great bravery of his men. He engaged and put to flight the French under Montcalm; but, to the great regret of the British, he was killed in the action nearly at the same instant that his adversary also fell. The surrender of Quebec was the consequence of this victory, and it was soon followed by the cession of all Canada. The next season, indeed, the French made a vigorous effort to recover the city; but by the resolution of Governor Murray, and the appearance of a British fleet under the command of Lord Colvile, they were obliged to abandon the enterprise. The whole province was soon after reduced by the prudence and activity of General Amberst, who obliged the French army to capitulate; and it has ever since remained as a dependency of the British empire. About the same time also the island of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUADALOUPE">Guadaloupe</a> was reduced by a force under Commodore More and General Hopson. At the beginning of the war the British affairs in Germany had worn a very unfavourable aspect. The Hanoverians were commanded by the Duke of Cumberland, who, greatly outnumbered by the enemy, was obliged to retire beyond the Weser. The passage of this river by the enemy might have been disputed with success; but the French were suffered to effect it unmolested. The Hanoverians were then driven from one part of the country to another, till at length they made a stand near a village called Hassenbach, where it was hoped the numbers of the enemy would not avail them in a general engagement. The Hanoverians, however, left the field of battle to the French, after a feeble resistance. The latter pursued, and the duke retired towards <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STADE">Stade</a>; by which means he marched into a country where he could neither procure <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> nor attack the enemy with any prospect of success. And here, being unable either to escape or advance, he was compelled to sign a capitulation, by which the whole army laid down their arms, and were afterwards dispersed into different cantonments. By this disgraceful surrender, which was called the capitulation of Closter Seven, Hanover was obliged to submit quietly to the French, and the latter were thus left at full liberty to turn their arms against the king of Prussia. Soon after this capitulation, both sides began to complain that the treaty had not been strictly observed. The Hanoverians exclaimed against the rapacity of the French general and the brutality of his soldiers. The French retorted the charge, accusing the Hanoverians of insolence and insurrection; and being sensible of their own superiority, resolved to bind them strictly to their terms of agreement. The Hanoverians, however, only wished for a pretence to take arms, and for a general to head them; and neither was long wanting. The oppressions of the tax-gatherers whom the French had appointed were considered as so severe, that the army rose to vindicate the freedom of their country; and Prince Ferdinand of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a> put himself at its head. As soon as this became known in Britain, large supplies were granted, both for the service of the king of Prussia, and for enabling the Hanoverian army to act vigorously in conjunction with him. A small body of British forces was sent over to join Prince Ferdinand under the Duke of Marlborough; but after some inconsiderable successes at Crevelt, the Duke of Marlborough died, and the command of the British forces devolved on Lord George Sackville. A misunderstanding, however, arose between him and Prince Ferdinand, the effects of which appeared at the battle of Minden, that was fought shortly after. Lord George, who commanded the British cavalry, pretended that he could not understand the orders sent him by the prince, and of consequence did not obey them. The allies gained the victory, but it would have been more decisive had the British commander obeyed his orders. He was soon after recalled, tried by a court-martial, found guilty of disobedience, and declared incapable of serving in any military command for the future. After this victory it was generally imagined that one reinforcement more of British troops would terminate the war in favour of the allies; and that reinforcement was accordingly sent. The British army in Germany was augmented to upwards of thirty thousand men, and sanguine hopes of conquest were generally entertained. But these hopes proved to be ill founded. The allies were defeated at Corbach, but retrieved the honour of their arms at Exdorf. A victory at Warbourg followed shortly after, and this was succeeded by another at Zierenberg. But they suffered a reverse at Compen; after which both sides retired into winter quarters. On the 25th of October 1760 died George II. He had risen at his usual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and observed to his attendants, that as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> was fine, he would take a walk into the garden of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KENSINGTON">Kensington</a>, where he then resided. But in a few minutes after his return, being left alone, he heard to fall heavily on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>; and the noise bringing his attendants into the room, they lifted him into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a>, when he desired in a faint <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> that the Princess <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMELIA">Amelia</a> might be sent for; but before she could reach the apartment his majesty expired, in the seventy-seventh year of his age and thirty-third of his reign. An attempt was made to bleed him, but without effect; and afterwards the surgeons, upon opening him, discovered that the right ventricle of the heart had been ruptured, and a great <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of blood discharged through the aperture. Bill.—Bill for the relief of the Dissenters rejected.—East India Affairs.—<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">Exportation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, and its consequences.—Regulation Bill.—Reports of the Select and Secret Committees.—Lord Clive accused.—His acquittal.—American King George III. ascended the throne amidst the greatest successes both by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>. At this time, indeed, the efforts of Britain in every <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe were truly astonishing. The king of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> had received a subsidy; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body of English forces commanded the extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of India; another <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of twenty thousand men confirmed the conquests in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> America, while thirty thousand were employed in Germany; and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many more were dispersed in garrisons in different parts of the world. But all this was surpassed by the naval force, which carried every thing before it, and totally annihilated the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> power. The courage and conduct of the English admirals excelled every thing that had been heard of before; neither superior force, nor numbers, nor even the terrors of the tempest, could intimidate them. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Hawke gained a complete victory over an equal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of French ships in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUIBERON">Quiberon</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Bretagne, in the midst of a storm, during the darkness of night, and, what a seaman fears still more, in the neighbourhood of a rocky shore. When his majesty had met his parliament, which was on the 18th November 1760, he confirmed the hopes of his allies, and gave assurances of his intention to prosecute the war with vigour. By this time, however, the people were weary of conquests, especially those in Germany; and the general current of popular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> seemed adverse to the German war. But for some time no change took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the method of carrying it on. In 1761, however, proposals of peace were interchanged among the belligerent powers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; but the French, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> to draw Spain into a confederacy with them, were not sincere in their intentions; and in this way the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> came to nothing. An enterprise was projected against Belleisle, on the coast of France, which was conducted by Commodore Keppel and General Hodgson, and terminated in the capture of the island, with the loss of eighteen hundred men killed and wounded on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the British; and however unimportant such a conquest might be, the rejoicings on account of it were great. In Germany, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> was unsuccessful on the part of the allies. At first, indeed, they drove the French out of the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, and laid siege to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Cassel; but being defeated at Stangerod, they were forced to raise the siege, retire behind the Dymel, and again abandon Hesse to the enemy, after which they were followed and attacked by the French; and though the latter were defeated, they could with difficulty be prevented from making themselves masters of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>. During all this time appearances of negociation were kept up; but at length M. Bussy, on the part of France, delivered to Mr Pitt a private memorial, signifying, that, in order to establish peace on a lasting foundation, the King of Spain might be induced to guarantee the treaty; and to prevent the differences which then subsisted between Britain and Spain from producing a fresh war in Europe, it was proposed, that in this negociation the three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which had been disputed between the crowns of England and Spain might be finally settled. These were, first, the restitution of some captures made upon the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>; secondly, a recognition of the privilege of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a> to fish upon the banks of Newfoundland; and, thirdly, the demolition of the English settlements in the Bay of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONDURAS">Honduras</a>. But this memorial was returned as wholly inadmissible.
