Mr Pitt declared that it would be looked upon as an affront to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and incompatible with the sincerity of the negociation, to make any further mention of such a circumstance. Being now convinced of the sinister designs of Spain, this minister also proposed immediately to declare war against that country. But the proposal being rejected, he resigned his employment of secretary of state; upon which he was created Earl of Chatham, and had a pension of L3000 per annum settled upon him for three lives. The new administration, however, soon found that Mr Pitt was in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; and war was accordingly declared against Spain. As Portugal was the ally of Britain, the French and Spaniards resolved to attack that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which was then in no condition to defend itself. The Portuguese monarch was haughtily commanded to accede to the confederacy against Britain, and threatened with the vengeance of France and Spain in the event of refusal. It was in vain that he promised to observe a strict neutrality, and urged the obligations he was under to the king of Britain. This moderate and reasonable representation only led to more haughty and insulting demands. His Portuguese majesty, however, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to reject their proposals in the most resolute manner; and concluded his last <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> by stating, that it would affect him less to be reduced to the last extremity, than to sacrifice the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and all that Portugal held most dear, by submitting to become an unheard-of example to all pacific powers, which would no longer be able to enjoy the benefit of neutrality, whenever a war should be kindled between other powers with which the former were connected by defensive treaties. This declaration was issued on the 27th of April 1762; and soon afterwards France and Spain jointly declared war against Portugal. As the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the courts of France and Spain in making war with Portugal was professedly to deprive Great Britain of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> and commercial <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the harbours of that kingdom, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> endeavours were directed against the two great ports of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OPORTO">Oporto</a> and Lisbon. With this view, three inroads were to be made; one to the north; another more to the south; and the third in the intermediate provinces, in order to sustain the other two bodies, and preserve a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between them. The first body of troops was commanded by the Marquis of Sávia, and entering by the north-east of Portugal, marched towards Miranda, which he entered on the 9th of May, through the breaches made by the accidental <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> of a powder <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>. From Miranda the invaders marched to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BRAGANZA">Braganza</a>, which speedily surrendered; and Moncorvo was in like manner taken. They became masters of nearly the whole of the extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Tras os Montes; and everything being clear before them to the banks of the Douro. Oporto was given up for lost, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> prepared transports to carry off the effects of the British <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. But on the Douro the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of this body was stopped by the peasants, who, animated and guided by some British officers, seized a difficult <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, and drove the enemy back to Moncorvo. The second body of Spaniards entered the province of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BEIRA">Beira</a>, and being joined by strong detachments, immediately laid siege to Almeida, which surrendered on the 25th of August. The Spaniards then pushed forward to Castello Branco, and marching to the southward, approached the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>. During the whole of their progress, and indeed throughout the whole campaign, Great Britain and Portugal had nothing that deserved the name of an army in the field; and all that could be done was by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of passes, by skirmishes, and by surprises. The third Spanish army had assembled on the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, with the design of invading the province of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a>; and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this body of troops had been joined to the others, they would probably, in spite of all opposition, have forced their way to Lisbon itself; whilst by acting separately, it might have so distracted the defenders of the country as to enable the other invading forces to penetrate to that city. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> of La <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-LIPPE">Lippe</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUCKEBURG">Buckeburg</a>, therefore, having arrived in Portugal, resolved if possible to prevent their entrance into that kingdom; and with this view he dispatched Brigadier-general Burgoyne to attack an advanced body of Spaniards which lay on the frontier in the town of Valenta de <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALCANTARA">Alcantara</a>. On the 27th of August the town was surprised, and the general who was to have commanded the invading force taken, together with one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a>, two captains, and seventeen subaltern officers, whilst one of the best regiments in the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> was also entirely destroyed, and the enemy thus prevented from entering Alentejo. That part of the Spanish army which acted in the neighbourhood of Castello Branco having made themselves masters of several important passes, the combined army of British and Portuguese pretended to retire before them, in order to draw them into the mountainous tracts. They attacked the rear of the allies, but were repulsed with loss; yet they still continued masters of the country, and nothing remained but the passage of the Tagus to enable them to take up their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> in the province of Alentejo. But this the count designed to prevent; and accordingly he employed General Burgoyne, who having formed a design of surprising them, committed the execution of it to Colonel <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEE">Lee</a>. In the night of the 6th of October this officer fell upon their rear, dispersed the whole body with considerable slaughter, destroyed their magazines, and returned with scarcely any loss. The season was now far advanced; immense quantities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> fell; the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> were destroyed; and the Spaniards having obtained possession of no advanced <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> where they could maintain themselves, and being unprovided with magazines, fell back to the frontiers of their own country. Nor were the British arms less successful in America and the East Indies. From the French were taken the islands of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARTINICO">Martinico</a>, St Lucia, St Vincent, and Grenada; from the Spaniards the strong fortress called Havana, in the island of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>. The conquest of the latter cost a number of brave men, more of whom were destroyed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> than by the enemy. But it was at this place that the fleets from the several parts of the Spanish West Indies, called the galleons and flota, assembled before they finally set out on their voyage for Europe; and the acquisition of it, therefore, united all the advantages which can be acquired in war. Nine of the enemy's men of war, with four frigates, were taken; three of their best ships had been sunk in the harbour at the beginning of the siege; and two more in great forwardness on the stocks were destroyed. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and valuable merchandises the spoil did not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short of three millions <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. To this success in the western world may be added the capture of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>-ship called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERMIONE">Hermione</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">Active</a> and Favourite king's ships. This happened on the 21st of May 1762, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> as the Hermione was entering one of the ports of Old Spain; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> was valued at little short of a million sterling. In the East Indies an expedition, undertaken against the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PHILIPPINE_ISLANDS">Philippine Islands</a>, was committed to Colonel Draper, who arrived on this service at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a> in the latter end of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1762. The seventy-ninth regiment was the only regular corps that could be spared for the expedition; but every thing was conducted with the greatest celerity and judgment. The British forces landed at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANILLA">Manilla</a> on the 24th of September; on the 6th of October the governor was obliged to surrender at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>; and soon after, the galleon bound from Manilla to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACAPULCO">Acapulco</a>, laden with rich merchandise to the value of more than half a million, was taken by the frigates Argo and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PANTHER">Panther</a>. By the conquest of Manilla there fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the British fourteen considerable islands, which, from their extent, fertility, and convenience for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, were of the greatest importance. By this acquisition, joined to the successes in the western hemisphere, Britain secured every avenue of the Spanish trade, and interrupted all communication between the different parts of the vast but unconnected empire of Spain. During this time the war in Germany had continued with the utmost violence; but although the allies under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Ferdinand had given the highest proofs of valour, no decisive advantage had been obtained over the French. It was, however, no longer the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Britain to continue a destructive contest. There never had been a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> so fortunate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> glorious for this island. In the course of the war she had conquered a tract of continent of immense extent. Her American territory approached to the borders of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and the frontiers of the Russian and Chinese dominions. She had conquered twenty-five islands, all of them distinguishable for their magnitude, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, or the importance of their situation; by sea and land she had gained twelve battles, and reduced nine fortified cities, and about forty castles or forts; she had taken or destroyed above a hundred ships of war from her enemies, and acquired at least ten millions in plunder. Conquests so extensive and ruinous to the French and Spaniards naturally rendered them desirous of a peace, which was at length concluded at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> on the 10th of February 1763. The terms granted, and which many thought too favourable, were, in substance, that the French king should relinquish all claims to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a>; that he should likewise give up the whole country of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>; and that for the future the boundary betwixt the British and French dominions in America should be fixed by a line drawn along the middle of the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a> from its source to the river Iberville, and thence by a line along the middle of this river, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">Lakes</a> Maurepas and Pontchartrain, to the sea. The islands of St Pierre, Miquelon, Martinico, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUADALOUPE">Guadaloupe</a>, Marigalante, Desirade, St Lucia, and Belleisle, were restored to France; whilst <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a>, Grenada, and the Grenadines, St Vincent, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMINICA">Dominica</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBAGO">Tobago</a>, were ceded to Great Britain. In <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, the island of Goree was restored to France; and the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, with all its forts and dependencies, ceded to Great Britain. In the East Indies, all the forts and factories taken from the French were restored. In Europe, the fortifications of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a> were to be destroyed; and all the countries, fortresses, and posts, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">Electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, the Duke of Brunswick, and the Count of La Lippe Buckeburg, restored. In regard to Spain, the British fortifications on the Bay of Honduras were to be demolished; and the Spaniards were to desist from their claim of right to fish on the Newfoundland bank. The Havana was restored, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, St Augustine, and the Bay of Pensacola, were ceded to Britain; the Spaniards were to make peace with Portugal; and all other countries not particularly mentioned were to be restored to their respective owners at the beginning of the war.

REIGN OF JAMES II

Pages 444-453

Accession of James II.—Slavish Addresses—Remarkable one by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>.—Imprudent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">Measures</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a>.—<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">Measure</a> in favour of the Catholics.—Monmouth's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">Conspiracy</a>.—Defeat and Execution of Argyll.—Landing of Monmouth.—<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">Battle</a> of Sedgemoore.—Defeat, Capture, and Execution of Monmouth.—James endeavors to establish <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>.—<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> dissolved.—Catholics promoted.—Opposition of the English Clergy.—An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> sent to Rome.—Declarations in favour of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">Bishops</a> imprisoned.—Popular commotions.—<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TRIAL">Trial</a> and acquittal of the Bishops.—<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">Attachment</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to the Protestant Cause.—Birth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>.—Treachery of Sunderland.—Proceedings of the Prince of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>.—Invited to England by the malcontents.—James warned of his danger by the French king.—Rejects all offers of assistance.—Parley by the news of the intended invasion.—Perfidy of Sunderland.—Vain attempt at a conciliation.—Landing of William Prince of Orange.—<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">Defection</a> of James's army.—Distressing situation of the King, who is deserted even by his own children.—Conduct of William.—James attempts to quit the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, but is seized and detained.—His distress.—Return to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>.—Ordered to leave the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>.—Urged to remain by some of his adherents.—His refusal.—Lands in France.—The throne declared vacant.—William raised to the Sovereignty in conjunction with the Princess <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> his wife. The first <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of James II.'s reign was to assemble the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, in which, after bestowing some praise on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his predecessor, he made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to maintain the established <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> both in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and state; and as he had heretofore ventured his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, he declared that he would still go as far as any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> in maintaining all its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges. This discourse was received with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause, not only by the council, but by the whole nation. Addresses came from all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, full of duty, nay, of the most servile adulation. From this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, however, must be excepted that of the Quakers, which is remarkable for its good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and simplicity. "We are come," said they, "to testify our sorrow for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of our good friend <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, and our joy for thy being made our governor. We are told that thou art not of the persuasion of the church of England, no more than we; wherefore we hope that thou wilt <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> us the same liberty which thou allowest thyself, which doing, we wish thee all manner of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>." The king, however, soon showed, either that he was not sincere in his promises, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> that he entertained so lofty an idea of his own regal power, that even his utmost sincerity could tend but little to the security of the liberties of the people. All the customs, and the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>, which had been voted to the late king for his life only, were levied by James without any new act for that purpose. He went openly to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> with all the ensigns of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and even sent one Caryl as his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> to Rome to make submissions to the pope, and to pave the way for the re-admission of England into the bosom of the Catholic church. By the suggestions of these men all his measures were undertaken. One <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> when the Spanish ambassador ventured to advise his majesty against putting too much confidence in such kind of people, "Is it not the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>," said James, "for the king to consult with his confessor?" "Yes," answered the ambassador, "and that is the reason why our affairs succeed so very ill." James's first parliament, which was composed mostly of zealous tories, was strongly inclined to comply with the measures of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and passed a unanimous vote, settling on James during life all the revenue enjoyed by the late king till the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his decease. For this favour James assured them that he would secure them in the full enjoyment of their laws: but with regard to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> no answer could be extorted from him, for that he was resolved at all hazards to change. In every thing except religion, however, James merited commendation. He applied himself to business with unremitting <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; he managed his revenue with the strictest economy; he retrenched superfluous expenses, and showed himself zealous for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the nation; he endeavoured to expel from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> the vice which had prevailed so much during the former reign, and to restore decency and morality; he presided daily at the council, and at the boards of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>; he even entered into the whole detail of the concern of the great departments of the state. But his bigoted attachment to the Roman Catholic religion sullied all his good qualities, and rendered him feared for his violence, where he was not despised for his weakness. But whilst every thing remained in tranquillity at home, a storm was gathering abroad. For a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> time the Prince of Orange had entertained hopes of ascending the British throne, and had even used endeavours to exclude James. Monmouth, who, since his last conspiracy, had been pardoned, but ordered to depart the kingdom, had retired to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he was received by the Prince of Orange with the highest marks of distinction, and became his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> favourite. When the news of Charles's death arrived, indeed, the prince made a show of changing his tone, and dismissed Monmouth, but still kept up a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> correspondence with him. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> retired to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>; and, having resolved to invade England, he was seconded by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Argyll, who formed the scheme of exciting an insurrection in Scotland. But the generosity of the Prince of Orange did not correspond with the warmth of his professions. The unfortunate duke derived from his own plate and jewels his whole supply for the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>; whilst the enthusiasm of a rich widow supplied Argyll with ten thousand pounds, with which he purchased three vessels, and loaded them with arms and ammunition. Having landed in Scotland, Argyll published his manifesto, put himself at the head of two thousand five hundred men, and strove to influence the people in his favour. But a formidable body of the king's forces having marched against him, his army fell away; and he himself, after being wounded in attempting to escape, was taken prisoner by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>, carried to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and, after suffering many indignities, publicly executed. By this time Monmouth had landed in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> with scarcely a hundred followers. His name, however, was so popular, and so great was the hatred of the people to James on account of his religion, that in four days he had assembled a body of above two thousand men, and continuing to make a rapid progress, in a short time found himself at the head of six thousand men; but he was daily obliged to dismiss great numbers for want of arms. Alarmèd at his invasion, the king recalled six regiments of British troops from Holland; and a body of regulars, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of three thousand, was sent, under the command of the Earl of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEVERSHAM">Feversham</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Churchill, to check the progress of the rebels. They took <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> at Sedgemoor, a village in the neighbourhood of Bridgewater, and were joined by considerable numbers of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>. Here Monmouth resolved to make a stand; and having drawn up his followers in the best order he could, he drove the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> infantry from their ground, and was on the point of gaining a complete victory, when the cowardice of Gray, who commanded the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, ruined all. This nobleman fled at the first onset; and the insurgents being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> in flank, gave way after a contest of three hours. About three hundred were killed in the engagement, and a thousand in the pursuit. Monmouth fled about twenty miles from the field of battle, till his horse sunk under him. He then alighted, and, exchanging clothes with a shepherd, fled on foot, attended by a German <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> who had accompanied him from Holland. Being at length quite exhausted with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and fatigue, they both lay <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in a field, and covered themselves with fern. Meanwhile the shepherd being found in Monmouth's dress, increased the diligence of the search; and by means of bloodhounds he was detected in his miserable situation, with raw peas in his pocket, on which he had subsisted for some days. He burst into tears when seized by his enemies, and petitioned, with abject importunity, for his life. He also wrote to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> dowager; he sent a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the reigning queen, as well as to the king himself; and he begged his life, when admitted into the presence of James, with a meanness unsuitable to his pretensions and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. But all his entreaties and submissions were of no avail. James told him that he was much affected at his misfortunes, but that his crime was too dangerous in its example to be left unpunished. In his last moments Monmouth behaved with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a> worthy of his former courage. When he came to the scaffold, he conducted himself with decency and even with dignity. He spoke little, he made no confession, nor did he accuse any of his friends. The circumstances attending his death excited horror among the spectators. The executioner missed his aim, and struck him slightly on the shoulder. Monmouth raised his head from the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, and looked him full in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a>, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> reproaching him for his mistake. The man struck twice again, but feebly, and then threw away the axe. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> forced him to renew his attempt; and the head of the duke, who seemed already dead, was at last severed from his body. Those concerned in the Duke of Monmouth's conspiracy were punished with the utmost severity. Immediately after the battle of Sedgemoor, Feversham hanged up above twenty prisoners, and was proceeding with his executions when the Bishop of Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a> informed him that these unhappy men were now by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> entitled to a trial, and that their execution would be deemed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. Nineteen were put to death in the same manner at Bridgewater by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Kirke, a man of a thoroughly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> and bloody disposition. This miscreant, practised in the arts of slaughter at Tangiers, where he had served in garrison, took <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in committing acts of wanton barbarity, and ravaged the whole country without making any distinction between friend and foe; his own regiment being designated, by way of eminence, "Kirke's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAMBS">Lambs</a>." The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> brutality of this man's temper was inflamed by continual intoxication. No fewer than eighty were executed by his orders at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DORCHESTER">Dorchester</a>; and on the whole, at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TAUNTON">Taunton</a>, and Wells, two hundred and fifty are computed to have fallen by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, as it was called, under the auspices of Judge Jefferies, who had been sent down to try the delinquents. This man, not satisfied with the sacrifice of the principals, charged the juries to search out the aiders and abettors of the rebellion; and those persons who, in compassion for the wretched fugitives, had afforded them an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, were denounced and punished as such. Even women did not escape, and two, Lady <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LISLE">Lisle</a> and Mrs Gaunt, were sentenced to be burned alive for similar acts of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. Jefferies, on his return from his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> in the west, was immediately created a peer, and soon after invested with the dignity of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>. In his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> James complains, with apparent indignation, of "the strange havoc made by Jefferies and Kirke in the west," and attributes the unpopularity which afterwards deprived him of the crown to the violence and barbarity of those pretended friends of his authority. James now began to throw off the mask, and to endeavour openly to establish popery and arbitrary power. He told the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Commons that the militia were found by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to be of no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; that it was necessary to augment the standing army; and that he had employed a great many Catholic officers, in whose favour he had thought proper to dispense with the test required to be taken by all who were employed by the crown. These stretches of power naturally led the Lords and Commons into some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of opposition; but they soon acquiesced in the king's measures, and then the parliament was dismissed for their tardy compliance. The parliament being dissolved, James's next step was to secure a Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the privy council. Accordingly four Catholic lords, Powis, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a>, Bellasis, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, were admitted as members. Sunderland, who <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that the only way to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> preferment was by popery, became a convert. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, was turned out of his office because he refused to conform. Even in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where the Duke of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a> had long supported the royal cause, this nobleman was displaced as being a Protestant, and the Lord Tyrconnel, a furious Catholic, was placed in his stead. In his zeal for popery, it is said that James stooped so low as even to attempt the conversion of Colonel Kirke; but the daring soldier told him that he was pre-engaged, for he had promised the king of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, when he was quartered at Tangiers, that if ever he changed his religion he would turn Mahommedan. At last the clergy of the church of England began to take the alarm, and commenced an opposition to court measures. The pulpits now thundered out against popery; and it was in vain that James attempted to impose silence on this topic. Instead of avoiding the controversy, the Protestant preachers pursued it with greater warmth. To effect his designs, the king determined to revive the High <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">Commission</a> Court, which had formerly given the nation so much disgust, and which had been abolished for ever by act of parliament. An <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> commission was Reign of accordingly issued, by which seven commissioners were invested with full and unlimited authority over the whole church of England. The next step was to allow liberty of conscience to all sectaries. This was done in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the Catholic religion would, upon a fair trial, gain the victory. Besides, the same power that granted liberty of conscience might restrain it; and the Catholic religion alone would thus predominate. He therefore issued a general <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, declaring that non-conformity to the established religion was no longer penal; but in Scotland he ordered his parliament to grant a toleration only to the Catholics, without interceding in the least for the other dissenters. In Ireland the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> were totally expelled from all offices of trust and profit, and Catholics put in their places. These measures sufficiently disgusted every part of the British empire; but to complete the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, James publicly sent the Earl of Castlemaine as ambassador extraordinary to Rome, in order to express his obedience to the pope, and reconcile his kingdoms to the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. This proceeding was too precipitate to be relished even by the pope himself; and therefore the only return he made to this embassy was the sending a nuncio into England. Soon after this the Jesuits were permitted to erect colleges in different parts of the kingdom, and to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the Catholic worship in the most public manner. In 1686 a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> in favour of liberty of conscience was published almost in the same terms with the former, but with this particular <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a>, that all divines should read it after <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in their churches. The clergy resolved to disobey this order. Lord, bishop of St Asaph, Kenn of Bath and Wells, Turner of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, Lake of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">White</a> of Peterborough, and Trelawney of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, together with Sancroft the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a>, concerted an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> in the form of a petition to the king, which, with the warmest expressions of zeal and submission, signified that they could not read the declaration consistently with their consciences or the respect they owed the Protestant religion. The king received their petition with marks of surprise and displeasure. He said he did not expect such an address from the church of England, particularly from some amongst them; and persisted in his orders for their obeying his mandate. As the petition had been delivered in private, the king summoned the bishops before the council, and there questioned them whether they would acknowledge it. They for some time declined giving an answer; but being urged by the chancellor, they at last owned the petition. On their refusal to give bail, an order was immediately issued for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMITMENT">commitment</a> to the Tower, and the crown lawyers received directions to prosecute them for a seditious <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a>. The king gave orders that they should be conveyed to the Tower by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was in commotion in their favour. But the people, when informed of their danger, ran to the river side in great multitudes, craving their blessing, and calling upon Heaven to protect them; whilst the very <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> by whom they were guarded kneeled down before them and implored their forgiveness. The 29th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1686 was fixed for the trial of the bishops. Twenty-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>, a great number of gentlemen, and an immense crowd of persons waited upon them to Westminster <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>. The discussion was learnedly managed by the lawyers on both sides. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JURY">jury</a> withdrew into a chamber, where they passed the whole night; but next morning they returned into court, and pronounced the bishops not guilty. Westminster Hall instantly rang with loud acclamations, which were communicated to the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the city, and even reached the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUNSLOW">Hounslow</a>, where the king was at dinner in Lord Feversham's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a>. His majesty demanded the cause of those rejoicings, and being informed that it was nothing but the soldiers shouting for the delivery of the bishops, "Call you that nothing?" said he; "but so much the worse for them." As the king found the clergymen everywhere averse to his measures, he was willing next to try what he could do with the army, thinking that if one regiment could be brought to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> implicit obedience, their example would soon induce others to comply. He therefore ordered one of the regiments to be drawn up in his presence, and desired that such as were against the late declaration of liberty of conscience should lay down their arms. He was surprised to see the whole battalion ground their arms, except two officers and a few Roman Catholic soldiers. A few days before the acquittal of the bishops the queen was delivered of a son. This, if any thing could at that time, might have served to establish James on the throne; but so violent was the animosity against him, that a story was propagated that the child was supposititious; and the monarch's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> scorned to take any precautions to refute the calumny. Though the enthusiasm of James himself was sufficiently extravagant, the wildest of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> projects seem to have been suggested by his enemies in order to accomplish his ruin. The Earl of Sunderland, whom he chiefly trusted, was a man of abandoned principles, insatiable avarice, and fitted by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> for stratagem, deception, and intrigue. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was his ruling <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and he accordingly sold his influence to the highest bidder. To such a degree was he mercenary, that he became at once the pensioner of the Prince of Orange and of the king of France. The former, who had long fixed his eye on the English throne, watched James's motions, and took every advantage of his errors. He had laid his schemes so extensively, that nothing but the birth of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> heir to the crown of England seemed likely to prevent him from obtaining an almost immediate possession of the kingdom; and he had the address to render two thirds of the powers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> interested in his success. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Augsburg, formed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the power of France, could not accomplish its object without the accession of England. The house of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, in both its branches, preferred their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> views to their zeal for the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and promoted the dethronement of James as the only means of humbling <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. Odescalchi, who under the name of Innocent XI, then filled the papal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, was also gained to the measures of the Prince of Orange by other considerations, as well as through his fixed aversion to France. Seeing the national discontent now raised to the highest pitch, the Prince of Orange resolved to take advantage of it. He began by giving one Dykerfelt, his envoy, instructions to apply in his name to every religious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in the kingdom. To the church party he sent assurances of favour and regard; protesting that his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in Holland had no way prejudiced him against Episcopacy. To the non-conformists he sent exhortations not to be deceived by the insidious caresses of their known enemy, but to wait for a real and sincere protector. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of these insinuations, the prince soon received invitations from the most considerable persons in the kingdom. Admirals Herbert and Russell assured him in person of their own and the national attachment. Henry Sidney, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to Algernon, and uncle to the Earl of Sunderland, came over to him with assurances of a universal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> against the king. Lord Danblanc, son to the Earl of Danby, being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a frigate, made several voyages to Holland, and carried from many of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> tenders of duty, and even considerable sums of money, to the Prince of Orange. Soon after, the Bishop of London, the Earls of Danby, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, Dorset, and several other lords, gentlemen, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> citizens, united in their addresses to him, and entreated his speedy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>. The people, though long divided between whig and tory, now joined against their misguided sovereign as against a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy. William therefore determined to accept their invitation; and this the more readily, as he perceived that the malcontents had conducted themselves with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and secrecy. Having the principal servants of James in pay, he was minutely informed of the most secret actions and designs of that prince. His intelligence came through Sidney from Sunderland, who betrayed the very measures which he himself had advised. The prince had a fleet ready to sail, and troops provided for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, before the beginning of June 1688. The king of France was the first who gave James warning of his danger, and offered to assist him in repelling it. But he declined this friendly offer, lest it should be said that he had entered into a private treaty with that monarch to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of the Protestant religion. Being also deceived and betrayed by Sunderland, he had the weakness to believe, that the reports of an invasion were invented in order to frighten him into a strict connection with France. He gave <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to the repeated assurances of the States, that the armament preparing in their ports was not designed against England; nay, he even believed the assertions of the prince himself, whose interest it was to deceive. Sunderland descended against the possibility of an invasion, and turned into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> all who believed the report. Having, with the consent of James, taken possession of all the foreign correspondence, he suppressed every kind of intelligence that might alarm; and all others whom James trusted, except <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARTMOUTH">Dartmouth</a>, affected long to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> no faith in the reports of an invasion. Louis finding his first offers rejected, next proposed to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">march</a> down his army to the frontiers of the Dutch provinces, and thus detain their forces at home for their own defence. But this proposal met with no better reception than the former one. Still Louis, unwilling to abandon a friend and ally whose interest he regarded as closely connected with his own, ventured to remonstrate with the Dutch against the preparations they were making to invade England. But the Dutch treated his remonstrances as an officious impertinence, and James himself declined his mediation. The king of England, having thus rejected the assistance of his friends, and being left to face the danger alone, was astonished with an advice from his minister in Holland, that an invasion was not only projected, but avowed. When he first read the letter containing this information, he grew <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and the letter dropt from his hand. He saw himself on the brink of destruction, and knew not to whom to apply for protection. In this emergency, Louis wrote to James in his own hand, that to divert the Dutch from their intended invasion of England, he would lay siege to Maestricht with thirty thousand men. James communicated this intelligence to Sunderland, and the latter to the Prince of Orange, by whom six thousand men were thrown into Maestricht; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of Louis being thus rendered impracticable, it was laid aside. James had now no resource but in retreating from those precipitate measures which had plunged him into inextricable distress. He paid court to the Dutch, and offered to enter into any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with them for their common security. He replaced, in all the counties of England, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> lieutenants and justices who had been deprived of their commissions for their adherence to the test and penal law. He restored the charters of such corporations as he had possessed himself of, annulled the High Commission Court, reinstated the expelled <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> and fellows of Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, and even caressed the bishops whom he had so lately persecuted and insulted. But all these concessions were now too late, and were regarded as the effects of fear, not of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, William set sail from Helvoetsluys with a fleet of near five hundred sail, and an army of about fourteen thousand men. Fortune, however, seemed at first very unfavourable to his enterprise. He was driven back by a dreadful storm; but he soon refitted his fleet, and again set sail for England. It was given out that this invasion was designed for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of France; and many of the English, who saw the fleet <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> along their coast, little suspected the place of its destination. It happened that the same <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> which sent the Dutch to their place of destination, detained the English fleet in the river; so that the Dutch passed the Straits of Dover without molestation, and, after a voyage of two days, landed at Broxholme in Torbay, on the 5th of November 1688, the anniversary of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. But although the invitation from the English was general, the prince for some time had the mortification to find himself joined by very few. He <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for ten days in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of being joined by the malcontents, and at last was beginning to despair of success, and to deliberate about re-embarking his forces, when he was joined by several persons of consequence; and the whole country soon afterwards flocked to his standard. The first person who went over to the prince was <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Burrington, and he was quickly followed by the gentry of the counties of Devon and Somerset. Sir Edward Seymour made proposals for an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>, which was signed by great numbers; and every day there appeared some new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of that universal combination into which the nation had entered against the measures of the king. This was followed by the defection of the army. Lord <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>, son to the Earl of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a>, first deserted to the prince; Lord Cornbury, son to the Earl of Clarendon, carried off the greatest part of three regiments of cavalry at once; and several officers of distinction informed Faversham their general, that they could not in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> fight against the Prince of Orange. Soon after this the unhappy monarch found himself deserted by his own servants and creatures. Lord Churchill had been raised from the rank of page, and had been invested with a high command in the army; he had been created a peer, and owed his whole fortune to the king's bounty; yet even he deserted among the rest, and carried with him the Duke of Grafton, natural son to the late king, besides Colonel Berkeley and others. In this universal defection, James, not knowing where to turn, began to think of requesting assistance from France, when it was now too late. He also wrote to Leopold, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Germany; but that monarch only returned for answer, that what he had foreseen had happened. James had some dependence on his fleet; but in reality they were entirely disaffected. In a word, his interests were deserted by all, for he had long deserted them himself. His army, however, still amounted to twenty thousand men; and had he led them immediately to battle, it is possible they might then have fought in his favour. But his misfortunes had deprived him of his natural firmness and resolution; and seeing himself deserted by those in whom he thought he could place most confidence, he became suspicious of all, and was in a manner deprived even of the power of deliberation. In this extremity of distress, the Prince of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, James's favourite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, perceiving the desperation of his circumstances, resolved to take part with the Prince of Orange. Informed of this event, the king was stung with the most bitter anguish. "God help me," said he; "my own children have forsaken me." To add to his distress as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, he was accused of being <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> to the death of his own child. On the 30th of November 1688, James dispatched three Reign of James II. noblemen to treat with the Prince of Orange. But though the latter knew very well that the king's commissioners were in his interests, his behaviour showed plainly that he now thought the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> for treating was past. For some time he would not admit them to an audience; and when he did, he gave no satisfactory answer. James now began to be alarmed for his personal safety; but what most affected him was the terror of the queen for herself and her infant son. He therefore resolved to send them abroad. They crossed the river in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, at Whitehall, on a stormy day, and were carried to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GRAVESEND">Gravesend</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, under the conduct of the Count de Lanzun; a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-YACHT">yacht</a>, commanded by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Gray, which lay there ready for the purpose, soon transported them in safety to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>. The king was now so dispirited and distracted, that he resolved to leave the kingdom at once, and thus plunge every thing in confusion. He threw the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>; he left none with any authority to conduct the government in his absence; and he vainly hoped to derive advantage to his affairs from anarchy and disorder. About twelve at night, on the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, he disguised himself, took a boat at Whitehall, and crossed the river. Sir Edward Hales, with another friend, met him at Vauxhall with horses. He mounted; and being conducted through by-ways by a guide, he passed in the night-time to the Medway, which he crossed by Aylesford-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. At Woolpeck he took fresh horses, sent thither before by Shelden, one of his equerries, who was in the secret of his flight. Having arrived at Emburyferry near Feversham, he found a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE">custom-house</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HOY">hoy</a>, hired by Sir Edward Hales, lying ready to receive him on board. But the wind blew fresh, and the vessel had no ballast. The master, therefore, easily persuaded the king to permit him to take in some ballast at Shilness. It being half ebb when they ran ashore, they intended to sail as soon as the vessel should be afloat; but when the vessel was almost afloat, she was boarded by three <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> boats belonging to Feversham, containing fifty men, who seized the king and his two companions, under pretence of their being Papists who wanted to escape from the kingdom. They turned up Feversham water with the tide; but still the king remained unknown. Sir Edward Hales placed privately fifty guineas in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the captain, as an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> of more should he permit them to escape. He promised, but so far from keeping his word, he took what money they had, under pretence of securing it from the seamen; and having possessed himself of their all, left them to their fate. The unfortunate fugitives were at length carried in a coach to Feversham, amidst the insults, clamours, and shouts of the sailors. When the king was brought to the inn, a seaman who had served under him knew him, and melted into tears; and James himself was so much moved at this instance of his affection, that he wept. The other fishermen, who had previously treated him with indignity, when they saw his tears, fell upon their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. The lower class of inhabitants gathered round him; but the better sort fled from his presence. The seamen, however, formed themselves into a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and declared, that "a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of his head should not be touched." In the mean time, Sir James Oxendon, under pretence of guarding him from the rabble, came with the militia to prevent his escape. The king found a change in his condition when he was taken out of the hands of the sailors. The commanders of the militia showed him no respect; and he was even insulted by the common soldiers. A letter which he intended to send to London for clothes, a change of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and some money, were stopped by those who pretended to protect his person. In the mean time the Prince of Orange exercised in his own person all the functions of royalty. He issued a declaration to the disbanded army to re-assemble themselves. He ordered the secretary at war to bring him a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the king's troops. He commanded the Lord Churchill to collect his troop of horse guards. He sent the Duke of Grafton to take possession in his name of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TILBURY">Tilbury</a> Fort. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of peers adjourned to the council-chamber at Whitehall, and, to give the appearance of legality to their meeting, chose the Marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> as their president. Whilst this assembly was sitting, on the 13th of December, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> countryman, who had been engaged by James, brought an open letter from that unfortunate prince to London. It had no subscription; and it was addressed to none. It described in one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> only, his deplorable condition when in the hands of a desperate rabble. This poor messenger of a fallen sovereign waited long at the council door, without being able to attract the notice of any who passed; but when the Earl of Mulgrave became apprised of his business, his lordship had the courage to introduce him to the council. He delivered his open letter, and told the unhappy state of the king. The assembly were much moved, and sent the Earl of Feversham with two hundred of the guards towards Feversham. His instructions were first to rescue James from danger, and afterwards to attend him to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> coast, should he wish to retire. He chose, however, to return to London; but the Prince of Orange sent a message to him, desiring him to approach no nearer the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> than Rochester. The messenger missed James by the way; and the king sent Feversham with a letter to the Prince of Orange, requesting his presence in London to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the nation, while he himself proceeded thither, and arrived on the 16th of December. The Prince of Orange received the news of his return with little satisfaction. His aim from the beginning was to force him by various means to relinquish the throne. The Dutch guards were ordered to take possession of Whitehall, and to displace the English; and the king was soon after commanded by a message, which he received in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a> at midnight, to leave his palace next morning, and to depart for Han, a seat of the Duchess of Lauderdale's. But he desired permission to retire to Rochester, which was readily granted. The harsh measures of the prince had now taken effect, and the king meditated an escape to France. Surrounded by the Dutch guards, he arrived at Rochester on the 19th of December. The restraint put upon his person, and the manner in which he had been forced from London, raised the indignation of many, and excited the compassion of all. The English army, both officers and soldiers, began to murmur; and had it not been for the timidity and precipitation of James himself, the nation would probably have returned to their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>. He remained three nights at Rochester, in the midst of a few faithful friends, the Earls of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARRAN">Arran</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a>, Allesbury, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>, and Middleton, and, amongst other officers of merit, Lord Viscount <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a>. They all argued against his intended flight; and several bishops, some peers, and many officers, entreated his stay in some part of England. They represented that the opinions of men began to change, and that events would daily rise in favour of his authority. Dundee added his native ardour to his advice. "The question, Sir," said he, "is, Whether you shall stay in England or fly to France? Whether you shall trust the returning zeal of your native subjects, or rely on a foreign power? Here you ought to stand. Keep possession of a part, and the whole <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> submit by degrees. Assume the spirit of a king. Summon your subjects to their allegiance. Your army, though disbanded, is not dispersed. Give me your commission. I will gather ten thousand of your troops. I will carry your standard at their head through England, and drive before you the Dutch..." First measures of William.—National discontent.—Scheme in favour of the Dissenters rejected.—Precarious condition of William's government.—Proceedings in Scotland.—William acknowledged as King.—Attempts of Viscount Dundee in favour of James.—Battle of Killiecrankie, and death of the Duke of Monmouth.—Insurrection in favour of James.—The Protestants take arms in their own defence, and are defeated at Drumore.—Landing of James in Ireland.—Subsequent operations.—Gallant defence of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LONDONDERRY">Londonderry</a>.—Odious measures resorted to by James.—Disembarkation of King William's army.—Its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>.—Arrival of William.—Battle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a>, and defeat of James.—Battle of Aughrim, and defeat of St Ruth, James's General.—Siege of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a>.—Pacification of Ireland.—Affairs of Scotland.—Massacre of Glencoe.—Conduct of William respecting this atrocious barbarity.—The Dower expedition.—Violent discontent in Scotland, in consequence of the supposed perfidy of the King.—Plots in favour of James.—James declares in his favour.—Battle of the Hoggs, and total defeat of the French fleet under Toronville.—James offered the crown of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, which he declined.—Offer by William to secure the succession to the Prince of Wales, James's son, also declined by him.—Death of James.—Conduct of Louis on this occasion.—The Pretender acknowledged by France as king of Great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and Ireland.—Death of Queen Mary.—National discontent.—William forced to disband his troops.—Altercations between the King and the Parliament.—Confederacy against France.—Death and Character of William. William began his reign with issuing a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> for continuing in office all Protestants who had been in place on the first of the preceding December. On the 17th of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> he formed his privy council, which consisted chiefly of those persons who had been most <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in raising him to the throne. To gratify as many as possible of his friends, the several boards, and even the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, were put into commission. The benches of the Exchequer and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS">Common Pleas</a> were filled with persons who had distinguished themselves against the measures of the late king. But the Earl of Nottingham, who had violently opposed the elevation of William, and the Earl of Shrewsbury, who had adhered to his views, were made secretaries of state. The Marquis of Halifax, and the Earl of Danby, though rivals in policy, were admitted into the cabinet; the first as lord privy seal, the second as president of the council. William's Dutch friends in the mean time were not forgotten by the king. Bentinck, his favourite, was made a privy counsellor, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GROOM">groom</a> of the stole, and privy purse; Auverquerque was appointed master of the horse; Zuylenstein received the office of master of the robes; and Schomberg was placed at the head of the ordnance. Though these instances of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> were no doubt necessary to William, the generality of the nation were displeased. The tories were offended at being excluded from favour, especially as they had departed from their usual principles in order to serve him. The nation in general were much prejudiced against foreigners, and universal discontent ensued upon seeing them preferred. The king, who had been bred a Calvinist, was also strongly inclined to favour that sect; and finding the clergy of the church of England but little inclined to take the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> to the new government, he began openly to indulge his own prejudices in favour of dissenters. Having come to the House of Lords to pass some bills, on the 16th March, he made a speech, urging the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of admitting all Protestants indiscriminately into the public service. He informed them, that he was employed in filling up the vacancies in offices of trust; he expressed his hopes that they had become sensible of the necessity of a law to settle the oaths to be taken by such persons as should be admitted into place; and he doubted not, that whilst they provided against Papists, they would at the same time leave room for the admission of all Protestants who were able and willing to serve their country. But this proposition was rejected with vehemence. The adherents of the church complained that the ruin which they feared from the Papists in the preceding reign was now to be dreaded from the Protestant dissenters; and they affirmed, that if the established religion was to be destroyed, it mattered little by whose hands it might <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BILL">bill</a> brought in by the ministry for abrogating the former oaths of supremacy and allegiance was rejected; and an attempt to dispense with the sacramental test was made without success in another form. The court party proposed that any man, by producing a certificate of his having received the sacrament in any Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>, should be held sufficiently qualified for office. But this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> was also rejected in the House of Lords by a great majority. William repeated his attempts at a comprehension; but he was ultimately unsuccessful, and in the coronation-oath the church party inserted a clause, that the king should maintain the Protestant religion "as established by law." For these and other reasons the government of William was for some time in a very tottering condition. The king, either through want of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> or inclination, interfered but little in the affairs of the nation; Ireland was strangely neglected; whilst Halifax and Danby, who had in a manner raised the king to the throne, caballed with his enemies. They perceived that the people, with the same levity which had induced them to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> their former sovereign, were beginning to be discontented with their new prince. Every thing seemed to tend to a change. Halifax himself declared, that were James to conform with the Protestants, he could not be kept four months from re-ascending his throne; and Danby averred, that were the late king to give satisfaction for the security of religion, it would be difficult to oppose his restoration. From these apparent discontents of the nation, the friends and emissaries of James assumed more boldness in tampering with the servants of the crown and inflaming the army. The former they alarmed with the prospect of a sudden change; the latter they roused into indignation by the alleged preference shown by William for his countrymen the Dutch. Though the kingdom of Scotland did not at first recognize the authority of William, yet the party of James never attained sufficient strength to be of any effectual service to him in that kingdom. Thirty Scottish Peers, and near eighty gentlemen, then in London, had waited on the Prince of Orange in the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; and, without any authority from the regency still subsisting in Edinburgh, formed themselves into a kind of convention. The Prince of Orange in a formal manner asked their advice; and when he withdrew, they adjourned to the council chamber at Whitehall. The Duke of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> being chosen president, explained the distracted state of Scotland, representing, that disorders, anarchy, and confusion prevailed, and urging the necessity of placing the power somewhere till a convention of estates should be called to form a lasting and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> settlement. When the heads of an address to the Prince of Orange had been settled, and ordered to be engrossed, the Earl of Arran unexpectedly arose, and proposed to invite back the king. The meeting, however, adhered to the Prince of Orange, and waited on him in a body, requesting him to take the administration into his own hands. He thanked them for the trust they had reposed in him; and a convention was ordered to meet at Edinburgh on the 14th of March, it being provided that no exception or limitation whatever should be made, except that the members should be Protestants. This convention, however, was opposed by some of the partisans of James; and the archbishop of Glasgow, the Earl of Balcarres, and the Viscount Dundee, were authorized by an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> signed by him, at that time in Ireland, to call a convention of the estates at Stirling. But this measure was disappointed, first by the wavering disposition of the Marquis of Atholl, and afterwards by the procrastination and folly of the party. At last Viscount Dundee, pretending alarm on account of a design alleged to have been formed by the Covenanters to assassinate him, left Edinburgh at the head of fifty horse. As he passed under the walls of the castle, the Duke of Gordon, who then held the command of the fortress, and favoured the cause of James, called him to a conference. Dundee scrambled up the precipice, and informed the duke of his designs in favour of James, at the same time conjuring him to hold out the castle, under a certainty of being relieved. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of the sight collected a multitude of spectators. The convention took the alarm. The president ordered the doors to be locked, and the keys to be laid upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. The drums <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> to arms in the town; and a parcel of ill-armed retainers were gathered together in the street by the Earl of Leven. Dundee in the meantime rode off with his party. But as soon as they found themselves secure, the Duke of Hamilton adjourned the convention, which relieved the adherents of James from dreadful apprehensions for their own safety. Fifty members retired from Edinburgh; and that circumstance produced unanimity in all the succeeding resolutions of the convention. Soon after this it was determined in a committee that James had "forefaulted" his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the crown, by which was meant that he had perpetually excluded himself and his whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a> from the throne, which was thereby become vacant. This resolution being approved by the convention, another was drawn up raising William and Mary to the vacant throne; and in consequence they were publicly proclaimed at Edinburgh on the 11th of April 1689. The castle of Edinburgh was still kept in the name of James by the Duke of Gordon; but despairing of any relief, and pressed by a siege, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> surrendered it on the 13th of June, upon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> terms. The adherents of James, terrified at this unexpected misfortune, now turned their eyes to the Viscount Dundee, who having been in vain urged by the convention to return, was at length declared a fugitive, an outlaw, and a rebel. General Mackay had been sent to Scotland by Williams, with four regiments of foot and one of dragoons. But Dundee, apprised of the general's design to surprise him, retired to the Grampian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a> with a few horse, and thence marched to Gordon Castle, where he was joined by the Earl of Dunfermline with fifty gentlemen.
